    One of many ways to interpret the U.S. midterm results is that they were an opportunity for Americans to express their concerns about the war in Iran. In that reading of events, Tehran’s strategy to hurt U.S. President Donald Trump has had at least some impact. But now that the elections are over, what will change? Will Trump feel like he now has no electoral constraints, widening his range of options in the war? And will Tehran feel like it has lost some leverage?

    According to Vali Nasr, a longtime Iran watcher, Iranian leaders believe that sustained disruptions to the global economy serve as a lever to change the actions of Western leaders—and perhaps act as a future deterrent. “Iran sees the result of the U.S. elections as proof of this concept. Their strategy is to boil the frog gradually,” he said on the latest episode of FP Live.

    Industry observers note that nasr is a professor and former dean of the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University. He is the author of, most recently, Iran’s Grand Strategy. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

    Ravi Agrawal: Let’s start with the U.S. point of view on the Iran war. The consensus has been that Trump has three options. He could escalate militarily, but that has very uncertain outcomes. He could spin a victory and get out, but the spin is . Or he could focus on diplomacy and try to return to the memorandum of understanding (MOU) we had last summer, but that is a lot of hard work. What do you think the White House strategy is now that the midterms are over?

    Vali Nasr: I think the president is actually pursuing all three strategies at the same time. Leaning in on diplomacy does not mean that he’s setting aside war prepares, and asking for war plans does not mean that he is doing less diplomacy. He doesn’t have any good choices.

    Ideally, Trump would end this war through a negotiated settlement, much like what happened in June, but he has to meet the Iranian price for doing that, which is actually quite steep for him. Presently, the positions of the two are too far apart. The Iranians want him to first go back to the MOU and implement it before they talk about anything else, such as the nuclear issue. Trump, on the other hand, needs the nuclear issue to be at the forefront in order to justify why he went to war for nine months.

    Industry observers note that war is also not really an option, because in order for war to be meaningful, Trump has to do something massive. But something big opens the door to Iranian retaliation, particularly in the Persian Gulf, which could devastate the global economy in larger ways. I’m sure Trump is hearing from Chinese President Xi Jinping and Arab, Chinese, and Russian leaders that nobody wants that kind of damage to the global economy. So he’s settling for the third option, which is to let Iran sit under the blockade and do nothing. In my opinion, that’s not a strategy. That’s twiddling his thumbs.

    Recent findings suggest that the blockade is not foolproof. Iran is getting oil out and making money. At the same time, the Strait of Hormuz is still under a lot of pressure. The Iranians have actually increased the number of attacks they’re making there. Furthermore, I don’t think it’s sustainable, financially or otherwise, for the U.S. Navy to maintain the blockade long term. It is quite financially and labor intensive for the Navy to do so, and it doesn’t have any bases in the Persian Gulf that could provide relief. If the Iranians are able to sustain themselves with the amount of holes that already exist, then, ultimately, this is not sustainable.

    Sources indicate that in fact, if the blockade starts working in the way in which the U.S. treasury secretary and U.S. secretary of state say it will, then Iran is likely to escalate. So ultimately, this strategy that everybody thinks is settled on is not tenable in the long term. Either it will collapse under its own weight, or one or the other party is bound to disturb it, which might bring us back to war.

    In a recent development, RA: I imagine that you could have noted a lot of this two weeks ago. The big change that has come in the last couple of weeks is, of course, the U.S. midterm election results. Come January, the Democrats will have power in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. They feel that part of the mandate from the American people is trying to find a way to end the war. What is your sense of how Congress might impact how Trump tries to prosecute the end of this war, or dilly-dally, as you said?

    In a recent development, VN: One outcome of these elections is a much more visible push within the United States against the war. It’s not just that the American people have spoken. If there was any shadow of a doubt that they really, really disliked this war, it has been dashed, particularly within the Republican Party. They might now think that if the Republican Party is to have any chance in 2028, this war should end now.

    Industry observers note that so there is a sense that there is more momentum for diplomacy after the election than there was before. In fact, when U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance wrote to Iran’s leadership, everybody stated, “That’s exactly what we thought the consequence would be of the drubbing the administration got.”.

    But Trump is unpredictable. He has his own view of what’s in his interest as well as what’s in America’s interest. He may go back to a conflict with Iran, so we’re not out of the woods. But the Iranians know that the economic cost of the war is having a tangible political impact on America, as well as France and Germany, even if it is not being reflected in the stock market on a daily basis. Ultimately, these countries are likely to decide at some point that this war is not worth the political blowback it’s causing.

    Industry observers note that RA: I was going to come to how Tehran is gaming out the post-midterms scenario. You make the point that Iran may sense that it is getting some of what it wants—it is imposing costs. The flip side of that could be that the costs have been imposed, and Trump has now seen the worst of it. He seems to be doubling down. With nothing to lose, he may now be impervious to electoral pressure, meaning the Iranians may not have much leverage with him.

    Sources indicate that VN: That’s very true. This is a gamble. It doesn’t mean that because the elections happened, the Iranians can declare victory and say, “OK, we humiliated President Trump, now let’s sit down and talk.” Yes, they had a substantial win in terms of the midterm results, but now they have to deal with Trump.

    I think the way they see it is that the decision to go to war is still uncomfortable for President Trump. It’s true that he’s not looking at another election, but the Republicans are looking at 2028. And ultimately, the longer this war goes on, the more the pressure it brings about, particularly if the next phase of the war is more destructive. The Iranians are broadcasting that loud and clear as a form of deterrence. They’re saying they’re going to wreak havoc on the region and the global economy, no holds barred.

    If that’s the case, then President Trump still has to think about his legacy. He has to think about the future of the Republican Party. And he has to consider that if he enters into a wider war with Iran and he still isn’t able to defeat it, the scale of his failure will be even greater than it is now.

    Until now, the most important factor on the American side hasn’t been some kind of a calculated, rational, technocratic national interest. It has been the psychology of one man from the get-go of deciding to go to war, to Trump’s various permutations.

    Nobody—whether it’s the United States’ allies or Iran or China—can say with any certainty how Trump might actually act. So I think the Iranians are taking this one step at a time, reading the tea leaves and applying pressure where they can with Congress—particularly the fresh Congress coming in—to see whether they can avoid a major war and get a settlement that would benefit them.

    The Iran war is most likely to end not with a bang, but with a whimper.

    The U.S. military faces “profound” long-term readiness concerns, one expert stated.

    Recent findings suggest that RA: Let me put something to you that I’ve been hearing from Trump administration officials I’ve spoken to on background. They say that Iran’s hand has significantly weakened over the last few months. The reasons they point to are that the amount of Gulf crude going through Hormuz has actually dropped significantly, from 83 percent to 60 percent, because Gulf states are using pipelines more and relying less and less on Hormuz. The rial is down to 1.7 million to the dollar. Recent U.S. sanctions have targeted the regime explicitly, as opposed to targeting the Iranian people. They’ve shut down parts of Mahan Air, which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) relied on, as well as a United Arab Emirates branch of Banque Misr, which served the IRGC.

    There’s a sense in the White House—or at least, it’s their narrative—that these measures must really hurt the people in power in Iran, and at some point the pain will be so great that the regime will be forced to make different choices. Do you buy any of that?

    Recent findings suggest that VN: No, I don’t. This is largely self-serving, anecdotal rhetoric, which has gotten us to this point. I don’t see a sign that the degree of pressure that this administration thinks it is imposing on Iran is actually being felt there and changing attitudes. When Iran sent its diplomats to the United Nations, the proposal they presented to the United States was an expansion of the Islamabad-brokered MOU, changed in ways that benefited Iran more. The Iranians referred to it as “Islamabad-Plus.”.

    According to recent reports, let’s also consider the fact that when Mecca defense alliance members and Pakistan’s army chief went to Tehran in October, Iran’s response to Vice President Vance’s letter was that Iran was sticking to its demands that Washington must fulfill all seven preconditions to resuming talks and reopening Hormuz. The United States’ pressure tactics are not working.

    Recent findings suggest that this administration doesn’t want to go to war or make a deal with Iran. They need to sell this “do nothing” strategy as a viable, working strategy, so they’re repackaging the blockade and saying it’s going to work this time. Two months ago, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was promising that there would be a run on the Iranian banks. That hasn’t happened. So I’m suspicious of these kinds of claims.

    According to recent reports, iran is under a tremendous amount of pressure, but I don’t think the administration has a gauge of where the tipping point for them is. So it’s throwing a Hail Mary pass with more sanctions, hoping that they will do the trick, and then we get a lot of rhetoric trying to sell the current holding pattern as an actual strategy.

    RA: So in response to everything you’re saying, Tehran’s strategy might be to wait out the next two years.

    It has been revealed that VN: If they have to, yes. Although, I don’t know. Iran’s supreme leader said in his last major statement that this “no war, no peace” situation is not sustainable or acceptable to Iran.

    According to recent reports, when and how will Iran disturb this status quo? We don’t know. We can already see that they are escalating pressure on shipping. In the past week, more of the shuttle ships that the UAE has been using to ferry oil from inside tankers in the Persian Gulf to tankers in the Arabian Sea are being hit. The number of mines installed in the Strait of Hormuz has also increased. More oil might go out on some days than others. So the Iranians are making the situation more unstable.

    There is a difference between the way the West and Iran look at this situation. The U.S. and many observers think a move from Iran has to be really substantial to be meaningful. For instance, if they can’t bring the cost of oil to $200 a barrel, then they’ve lost.

    But the Iranians actually do not look at things this way. Very early in the war, they understood that the price of oil is not 100 percent in their hands. What they believe works is sustained instability in the energy market. The costs of oil, natural gas, jet fuel, diesel, fertilizer, and so on are far above where they were. None of these measures by themselves will break the global economy, but if you put them together for long enough, they’re very effective.

    Iran sees the result of the U.S. elections as proof of this concept. Their strategy is to boil the frog gradually. I think sometimes in the West we look at this and say, “Well, the frog is just sitting there and nothing’s happening to it, so the Iranians have failed.” So I think this is a race between whether Iran runs out of gas first or its strategy works.

    Right now, I detect a certain degree of confidence from Iran. I don’t see the trepidation that observers on the outside are assuming the regime has. So either Iran has a good poker face, or it’s seeing the picture very differently than Washington does.

    RA: It’s fascinating, and it’s always so hard to know whom or what to believe.

    I’m curious what you make of these reports that claim to be from U.S. intelligence suggesting that Iran is developing prepares to detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C. These are just reports. Tehran, of course, denies that any of this is true, but I’m curious how you are reading that story and reacting to it.

    VN: We’re in the midst of a war, and there’s a lot of disinformation. There are people in the United States or in Israel who want the United States to go back to war with Iran, to “finish the job,” so to speak. After the elections, which made it very obvious that the American public is firmly opposed to this war, you could only change that public opinion in favor of war if there was this kind of threat against America, or if you could posit that Iran is a deranged and crazy regime that must be taken out. So it could possibly be disinformation.

    According to recent reports, on the other hand, Iranians have also been taking certain actions as a form of deterrence. I don’t know whether Iran actually launched a cyberattack on refrigerators in France—French intelligence claims they did, though the Iranians deny it—but it’s a message. “If you attack us, then we have cyber capabilities that could paralyze your cities.”.

    Sources indicate that it’s a kind of deterrence tactic. It’s a similar case with Iran issuing warnings to air bases in the U.K., which ultimately got the United States to move its airplanes from two different air bases. Some of this benefits Iran, because it’s a way of saying, “Do not assume that the next war would be cost-free. Our reach is much farther than you assume.”.

    It also suggests to me that Iran doesn’t want to go back to war. Rather, its game blueprint is to try to get the United States to come to the table to accept their terms.

    Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

    • Industry observers note that stephen E.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    STEPHEN E. BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    And Now He Needs a Latest Strategy.

    Industry observers note that stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery.

    Industry observers note that donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind. In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump announced that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”.

    It has been revealed that trump has not been subtle about his desire to restart diplomacy with Kim. With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win. During his first term, Trump held two historic U.S.–North Korean summits aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula—but both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal. Since his reelection, Trump has been looking to reopen talks with Kim. The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court, and Kim has signaled, if not an eagerness for renewed engagement, at least an unwillingness to rule it out. In August, after Trump insisted for the second time that he was in touch with Pyongyang, Kim Yo Jong—the leader’s influential sister—released a statement that read: “Regarding the reports from Washington about recent communication between the top leaders of North Korea and the U.S., I am completely unaware of such matters. It has been stated on numerous occasions that our head of state holds fond personal memories and positive feelings toward Trump. The relationship between the leaders remains excellent.” Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

    According to recent reports, if leader-to-leader talks materialize, Trump may believe his personal rapport with Kim will yield a deal. But he will be facing a very different North Korea than the one at their last meeting in 2019. The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand. Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.

    For a U.S.–North Korean summit to be successful, the United States must approach it with well-defined strategic goals and a clear understanding of what concessions it is willing to make. Washington should shift its focus away from denuclearization, at least in the short term, to concentrate on more achievable nuclear arms control and safety measures. The United States should also maintain a capable troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and reiterate its security assurances—particularly its nuclear-deterrence guarantees—to regional allies such as South Korea and Japan.

    In a recent development, although diplomacy with North Korea has historically been difficult, Trump is eager to meet with Kim, and both sides want to avoid pushing the Indo-Pacific toward nuclear proliferation or all-out war. Careful engagement with Pyongyang could defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula and lay the groundwork for a more stable security landscape.

    In a recent development, since the U.S.–North Korean summit in 2019, the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have reshaped the Indo-Pacific in ways that strengthen Kim’s hand. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has drawn Washington’s focus away from Asia as, for the third time in the past quarter century, U.S. strategic attention and military assets have surged to the Middle East. The last American aircraft carrier stationed in the Indo-Pacific departed for the Persian Gulf in August, and U.S. strikes on Iran have rapidly depleted American munitions stockpiles. Washington’s Indo-Pacific allies, already strained by Trump’s abrupt policy shifts and punishing tariffs, are now concerned about deteriorating deterrence. Asian economies—many of which are deeply dependent on Middle Eastern energy supplies—have contracted as the Strait of Hormuz has remained compromised. Amid signs of further American retrenchment, U.S. allies and partners are increasingly skeptical about Washington’s commitment to the region.

    It has been revealed that even more consequential is Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which has benefited North Korea in numerous ways. Moscow and Pyongyang’s once dormant relationship has flourished as Kim has sent thousands of munitions to replenish Russia’s depleted stockpiles and thousands of soldiers to fight and die in the ongoing ground war. Images of the new memorial to the Korean People’s Army soldiers who have perished in the invasion suggest an already significant loss of North Korean lives. In return, Pyongyang has received generous assistance from Moscow in violation of international sanctions, including abundant financial support for Kim’s regime and technology transfers that have enhanced North Korean military capabilities and may help Pyongyang more accurately deliver intercontinental ballistic missiles aimed at the United States. Russian patronage allows Kim to shower his regime’s elites with the economic benefits needed to cement their loyalty.

    According to recent reports, still, it is worth questioning how durable this partnership is. After more than four years of grinding warfare with no end in sight, Moscow is increasingly isolated and may be in a poor position to continue supporting Pyongyang. Russia’s preoccupation with Ukraine has allowed China to expand its presence in Central Asia, for instance, and Turkey to deepen its influence in Azerbaijan. Russian aggression has spurred Armenia and Moldova to look westward, and hundreds of thousands of young Russian men have fled the country to avoid military conscription while over a thousand Western companies have left. International sanctions are starving Russia of badly needed capital and technology, and Russian war policies have created huge imbalances and inflation, possibly with worse to come for the Russian economy. If North Korea continues to actively support Moscow in this war, and Russia fails or is defeated, the world will become a much more hostile place for Pyongyang.

    Russia and North Korea’s deepening ties have already begun to reshape China’s interests in the region. Beijing is still Pyongyang’s most important partner, but the dynamic has changed considerably in recent years. Beijing previously saw denuclearization as a top priority on the Korean Peninsula—a shared objective, and at times a rare area of cooperation, with the United States. It disliked the destabilizing impact that North Korea’s pursuit of nuclear weapons had on tensions between the North and South and expended political capital responding to international condemnation of Pyongyang. Between 2006 and 2017, Beijing agreed to a series of UN Security Council resolutions that imposed sanctions and other restrictions on Pyongyang in response to six North Korean nuclear tests. Now, pressed to maintain its influence in Pyongyang amid a growing Russian–North Korean security relationship—and with the rest of the world distracted by other geopolitical crises—China has gone silent on the issue. When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June to reassert his influence, denuclearization was not publicly mentioned. China’s newly introduced approach will make U.S. engagement on this issue more challenging and risks driving other regional powers, such as South Korea and Japan, to reconsider their own policies on the deployment or development of nuclear weapons.

    Recent findings suggest that whether Pyongyang reengages with the United States may also depend on how much North Korea relies on China for economic support. Much of North Korean commerce passes through China, and although Beijing and Pyongyang’s relationship appears fairly stable, it remains wary and transactional, with each side skeptical of the other’s motives. North Korea may seek to reengage with the United States to counterbalance its overdependence on China, or as a hedge against Russia’s failure in its war with Ukraine. Conversely, as Trump and Xi upgrade and stabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, China could step in to broker the next Trump-Kim meeting.

    It has been revealed that the Kim dynasty has long vexed U.S. policymakers. Washington has sought multiple deals with North Korea, including during Trump’s first-term summits with Kim, but missteps and mistrust on both sides derailed them. Pyongyang has proved resilient to both U.S. and international sanctions. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and deprived itself far more severely than sanctions could, yet it still survived. U.S. congressional interventions on human rights and humanitarian aid, meanwhile, have mostly failed to change North Korea’s behavior. Pyongyang has also cushioned the impact of sanctions by engaging in cybertheft, such as its $6.3 billion heist against the cryptocurrency exchange Binance this October. All the while, Pyongyang has steadily advanced its military capabilities and expanded its nuclear arsenal.

    Recent findings suggest that although Washington’s previous attempts to rein in North Korea have failed, Trump’s renewed eagerness to meet with Kim and his unorthodox approach to foreign policy could provide a latest opening for diplomacy. Trump has cultivated a direct relationship with Kim, shunning the bureaucratic negotiations that usually precede a deal. While a performative summit alone would be of little benefit to U.S. interests, Washington could use reengagement with Pyongyang to thaw inter-Korean relations and stabilize the peninsula by slowing or freezing North Korea’s nuclear buildup. Those goals may seem conventional, but as regional tensions worsen and Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal grows, they are essential to averting potentially catastrophic conflict.

    Three questions cast a shadow over the possibility of renewed engagement between the United States and North Korea. First is the specific purpose of restarting engagement: What is the goal? Second is how to reopen communications. Despite Trump’s claims, there is no real proof that he has recently interacted with Kim. All evidence suggests the last contact between American and North Korean officials was in 2019, and it may be challenging to break a seven-year drought. Third is what are the incentives and tradeoffs the United States would be willing to consider as part of a negotiation—the same concern that bedeviled U.S. and North Korean officials in Hanoi.

    One possible formula for progress is focusing, at least temporarily, on steady arms control and international safety controls rather than the elusive goal of denuclearization. Denuclearization should remain Washington’s ultimate aspiration. But in the meantime, a North Korea awash with even more nuclear weapons makes the world only more dangerous. This approach will require serious diplomacy to minimize second-order consequences, particularly to avoid weakening U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific or triggering a collapse of the nuclear nonproliferation regime among nations that might see their only recourse as acquiring their own nuclear weapons. China, and perhaps even Russia, may concur with Washington on this point, and a shared desire to avoid more nuclear states in East Asia could help restart engagement.

    Industry observers note that kim has substantially more leverage now than in earlier encounters with Trump. Reopening communication will require using a mix of positive and negative assurances to convince him that he is unlikely to get a better chance to strike a deal. Kim may press the United States to scale back aspects of its cooperation with South Korea—such as joint military exercises and support for Seoul’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines—as preconditions for a meeting with Trump. Kim may even propose his own assurances of peace on the peninsula in exchange for a reduction of U.S. military forces in South Korea, although it is unclear whether Trump would agree to such conditions.

    In the worst-case scenario, Kim may take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to make a deal to extract weighty concessions from the United States. Kim has little reason to meet with Trump now, unless he calculates that he can secure major terms such as de facto recognition as a nuclear state, reduced sanctions, or a complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the peninsula. Kim would likely insist that there be no discussion of denuclearization, North Korea’s support for the invasion of Ukraine, Pyongyang’s human rights abuses, or a final accounting for Japanese citizens kidnapped by North Korea under the rule of Kim Il Sung. Granting such concessions would end the U.S.–South Korean alliance.

    To ensure North Korea does not exploit the Trump administration, Washington must carefully consider what tradeoffs it is willing to make. Lifting sanctions, abandoning or delaying the denuclearization process, temporarily accepting North Korea as a nuclear state, and reducing the U.S. military presence in South Korea are all long-standing demands of Kim’s regime that are likely on the table. Although lifting international sanctions would require UN Security Council consensus, Trump may be willing to reduce unilateral U.S. sanctions, which he considers an obstacle to better bilateral relations and which have been ineffective in stemming Pyongyang’s nuclear advances.

    Recent findings suggest that although denuclearization has been a major talking point for U.S. administrations since the early 1990s, the Trump administration may need to set it aside, at least in the short term. Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities have increased since Trump’s 2018 and 2019 summits with Kim, suggesting that the stalemate caused by continued U.S. demands for the full-scale dismantlement of North Korea’s nuclear program may have given Kim time and space to grow his arsenal. Even if denuclearization remains a long-term U.S. priority—and it should—pragmatism is essential to reducing the threat posed by Kim’s regime. In exchange for stepping away from denuclearization, Trump should demand that Kim freeze any further expansion of his arsenal and explore possibilities for greater strategic stability, including renewed inter-Korean dialogue, transparency and confidence-building efforts, security measures that bolster nuclear facilities’ safety and guard against accidents, and strict adherence to nonproliferation. Trump must make it clear to Kim that an unconstrained expansion of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal will pressure South Korea and Japan to deploy nuclear weapons on their territory and possibly develop their own.

    Industry observers note that regardless of Kim’s demands, the United States must preserve its troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and continue joint military exercises with South Korea as long as the threat of North Korean aggression persists. The mantra of U.S. troops in South Korea is “ready to fight tonight.” Joint military exercises keep U.S. and South Korean forces prepared for combat, which is essential to deterring North Korean attacks. It would be dangerous and irresponsible to send American soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen to the peninsula without ensuring peak readiness. Instead of withdrawing troops, the United States should offer confidence-building measures to North Korea—practices that reduce the risk of conflict breaking out because of misjudgment. These could include military-to-military engagement and security reassurances among the United States, South Korea, and North Korea, or greater transparency around military exercises—allowing observers on a reciprocal basis, for example. Sustaining Washington’s alliance with South Korea and avoiding cascading nuclear proliferation are critical to U.S. interests in the region. American negotiators must remind Kim that the U.S. military presence and its extended nuclear-deterrence guarantees for Seoul and Tokyo hold back even larger conventional military—and possibly nuclear—buildups in the region.

    According to recent reports, finally, North Korea and the United States—and perhaps, in time, South Korea and Japan—should sustain diplomatic engagement by agreeing to assign diplomats to each other’s capitals through reciprocal liaison offices, which would maintain relations without granting full diplomatic recognition. In 2018 and 2019, the two sides discussed housing such diplomats in the German Embassy in Pyongyang and the Swedish Embassy in Washington. Liaison offices would also stabilize and prolong the communication necessary to quietly work through complex negotiations.

    It has been revealed that if North Korea rejects Trump’s overtures, the United States is not without options. Washington could pressure the Kim regime by intensifying the scale and tempo of joint military exercises with South Korea; deploying American armaments, including short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and possibly nuclear weapons, to South Korea and Japan; and pursuing a newly introduced campaign to choke off North Korea’s economic resources through sanctions and interdiction. The United States could also deploy additional air defense assets to Japan and South Korea, including THAAD air defense radar systems and interceptors. Washington and its allies could dramatically expand efforts to undermine Kim’s rule by mounting sustained criticisms of North Korea’s dangerously large nuclear weapons arsenal and its use of international criminal enterprise to steal from and economically defraud other nations, which could spur other countries to curb their material or diplomatic support for North Korea or more aggressively sanction Kim’s regime.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond short-term negotiations, a fourth question is less complicated but just as key: What role should Japan and South Korea play in U.S. engagements with North Korea? Many past administrations, both Republican and Democratic, have considered coordination with allies essential to establishing a durable solution on the Korean Peninsula. But Trump’s antipathy toward alliances suggests close consultation with South Korea and Japan is unlikely. Their absence from the negotiating table may actually accelerate U.S.–North Korean engagement, because coordination across allied governments can be unwieldy and slow, and Pyongyang has not been receptive to past overtures by Seoul and Tokyo. Although South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi both rhetorically back engagement with North Korea, Pyongyang has bluntly rejected their outreach.

    Industry observers note that even if Seoul and Tokyo are not directly engaged in U.S.–North Korean diplomacy, they would still likely welcome a U.S.-led deal with Kim if it protects their core security interests. But a deal with Kim that ignores American allies’ concerns would be dangerous. South Korea harbors an appetite to develop its own nuclear arsenal, particularly if it feels U.S. security protections are receding. Should Seoul move in that direction, Tokyo would almost certainly reconsider its own nonnuclear status, potentially igniting a nuclear arms race in Asia. Given North Korea’s long-standing hostility toward both Japan and South Korea, proliferation would destabilize the Indo-Pacific and leave the global nonproliferation regime in tatters.

    Any deal, even one that addresses Seoul’s and Tokyo’s core interests, will likely need to be paired with American security reassurances to allies’ governments and publics. Japan and South Korea must continue building their own conventional defense capabilities while the United States sustains its commitment to defending its Asian allies—especially extended nuclear deterrence. The United States must pursue delicate, nuanced diplomacy to avoid creating a stronger, legitimized North Korea; straining its alliances with Seoul and Tokyo; and debilitating the international nonproliferation regime.

    Despite the risks of U.S.–North Korean engagement, the time may be ripe to break the diplomatic paralysis that has allowed Pyongyang to advance its military capabilities for so long. The last two years of Trump’s presidency—particularly his summitry calendar in late 2026—will bring him to Asia, potentially facilitating a meeting with Kim. Such a visit would present the best chance for the kind of performative, high-profile meeting that both Trump and Kim favor.

    According to recent reports, trump is the ultimate iconoclast in traditional great-power politics, as evidenced by his shifting relationships with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which could shape Washington’s engagement with Pyongyang. Still, there may be a way to leverage Trump’s affection for Kim, and Kim’s recent restraint in criticizing the United States, to outline a deal that arrests the growing threat of North Korean nuclear weapons.

    Recent findings suggest that the bruising Republican defeat in the U.S. midterm elections could also change North Korea’s diplomatic calculus, especially because it suggests Trump’s political standing in the United States has faltered, and he may struggle to deliver the results Kim seeks. Trump may force the matter, however, and propose a meeting with Kim after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China. It would not be surprising for Trump to suggest that this meeting take place in Pyongyang, putting Kim on the spot. If leader-to-leader talks occur, both sides should remember the central lesson from Trump’s first-term summits: engagement without sufficient preparation and clearly defined goals is not enough to strengthen security and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

    It has been revealed that growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific raise the prospect of a much darker future, where conditions on the Korean Peninsula remain unchanged and Asia’s entanglements in European and Middle Eastern conflicts metastasize into a new world war—perhaps ignited in Taiwan, the South China Sea, or the Korean Peninsula. Even if no war breaks out, in just a few years the United States could find itself in a world where Asia’s five current nuclear states are joined by two, three, or more new players.

    According to recent reports, but this future is not inevitable. All the leaders engaged in North Korean security debates—from Lee and Takaichi to Xi and Putin—want to avoid such escalation. Even the North Koreans surely recognize this is the most dangerous path. This shared goal means diplomacy is still possible, despite formidable challenges. For all Trump’s idiosyncrasies, one should take his desire to peacefully end tensions on the Korean Peninsula at face value. He has made his intentions clear. What happens next is up to Chairman Kim.

    OMCO Solar offers solar-powered tracker control system

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OMCO Solar now offers a version of its OMCO Star Tracker Control System powered entirely by solar energy, allowing tracker controls to operate without AC power at the site.
    • The system, first launched last year, is designed for OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers.
    • Sources indicate that according to OMCO, the technology eliminates the need for AC power to tracker control components and an uninterruptible power supply.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OMCO Solar now offers a version of its OMCO Star Tracker Control System powered entirely by solar energy, allowing tracker controls to operate without AC power at the site.

    The system, first launched last year, is designed for OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers. Its tracker controllers, array controllers and sensor bridges use all-weather battery packs charged by solar modules.

    Sources indicate that according to OMCO, the technology eliminates the need for AC power to tracker control components and an uninterruptible power supply. It also allows tracker controls to operate and protects modules against wind, snow and hail before AC power is available.

    Sources indicate that “Our industry has solved so many problems as we have grown – we’re now the leading source for fresh electric energy capacity in the US. This addition to the OMCO Star product line solves one more – how to protect modules if there’s no AC power to the site even for a short time. We’re excited to offer this solution to our existing customers and to new partners,” said Matt Kesler, vice president of solar technology at OMCO Solar, in a statement.

    Sources indicate that the OMCO Star system uses LoRa, or long-range, wireless technology with a communication range greater than 1 mile. According to OMCO, this reduces the number of network controllers required and allows direct communication with every tracker without relying on a mesh network.

    The organization indicates LoRa is 100 times less susceptible to electromagnetic noise than Zigbee and better able to connect to distant trackers despite obstacles.

    Recent findings suggest that OMCO says its all-weather battery packs allow the solar-powered controls to operate reliably in cold climates. The system includes field-replaceable batteries, a phone app that eliminates the need for buttons on controllers and a remote monitoring and control portal.

    Recent findings suggest that the portal allows operators to move trackers for activities such as mowing, snow plowing and module cleaning. The system is developed, manufactured and supported by OMCO Solar in the United States.

    It has been revealed that “We are excited about bringing this innovation to the Utility Scale and DG tracker markets. Over the past few years, OMCO has expanded its capabilities beyond just being a US steel manufacturer to now being a true technology leader in our space. We look forward to supporting our customers/partners with the OMCO Star Tracker Control System, improving reliability, and reducing the labor and materials needed to build their projects,” said Eric Goodwin, vice president of business development at OMCO Solar.

    OMCO Solar will display the all-DC tracker control system at RE+ in Las Vegas, November 17–19, in the North Hall, booth N516.

    In Italy, Meloni Grapples With a Potential Spoiler

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni celebrated the fourth anniversary of her government with a large rally in the port city of Bari in September.
    • Sources indicate that A pamphlet handed out at the Bari rally highlighted Meloni’s economic and immigration policies, a major public housing initiative, proposals to build fresh prisons, and a push to reintroduce nuclear power.
    • Sources indicate that italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni celebrated the fourth anniversary of her government with a large rally in the port city of Bari in September.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    According to recent reports, italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni celebrated the fourth anniversary of her government with a large rally in the port city of Bari in September. Her administration is now the longest-serving in Italy—and the most far-right—since World War II. Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy party, rules in a coalition with the populist League and center-right Forza Italia.

    Sources indicate that A pamphlet handed out at the Bari rally highlighted Meloni’s economic and immigration policies, a major public housing initiative, proposals to build fresh prisons, and a push to reintroduce nuclear power. Missing among the milestones was any mention of Italy’s support for Ukraine.

    Sources indicate that italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni celebrated the fourth anniversary of her government with a large rally in the port city of Bari in September. Her administration is now the longest-serving in Italy—and the most far-right—since World War II. Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy party, rules in a coalition with the populist League and center-right Forza Italia.

    Recent findings suggest that A pamphlet handed out at the Bari rally highlighted Meloni’s economic and immigration policies, a major public housing blueprint, proposals to build fresh prisons, and a push to reintroduce nuclear power. Missing among the milestones was any mention of Italy’s support for Ukraine.

    It has been revealed that that absence is no coincidence. Meloni is now grappling with a challenger further to her right on many complications: Roberto Vannacci, a former general who leads the ultranationalist, pro-Russian National Future party. His influence is putting the prime minister in a difficult position with voters and shaping her political choices, especially on Ukraine—already seen as a weak point for Meloni.

    Vannacci rose to national prominence in 2023 with a bestselling self-published book, The World Upside Down, that railed against LGBTQ rights, feminism, immigration, and environmentalism. He was elected to the European Parliament the next year with the League, but in January, he left the party to found his own.

    Amid pressure from Vannacci and his party, Meloni’s government has hardened its line on immigration; passed law-and-order measures targeting violent protests, vandalism, and illegal gatherings; and expanded legal protections for police. The prime minister also backed a controversial antisemitism bill, approved by Parliament this week, that opponents say conflates criticism of Israel with anti-Jewish sentiment.

    Sources indicate that until recently, Meloni had no serious rivals, and her Brothers of Italy party led every poll. Though Vannacci’s National Future is now losing some ground, he could still serve as a spoiler for Meloni. Her party’s rightward shift could even hand the divided center-left an unexpected victory in the general elections that are due next year.

    Brothers of Italy, which Meloni co-founded in 2012, has roots in the former Italian Social Movement (MSI)—a neofascist party that emerged from the remnants of Benito Mussolini’s regime in 1946. Meloni has never disavowed those origins, arguing that MSI was a “party of the democratic right” even as she has distanced herself from historical fascism.

    According to recent reports, meloni’s coalition partners have helped her project that image of distance, to varying degrees. Forza Italia, which is a member of the center-right European People’s Party, defines itself as the moderate wing of the coalition. The League doesn’t have fascist roots but tries to outflank Brothers of Italy on the right on certain issues.

    Sources indicate that for the past 30 years, no far-right party has succeeded as a permanent force in Italy outside of the center-right coalition. Elsewhere in Europe, the far right has solidified its presence and destabilized mainstream politics—including the National Rally in France, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, and Britain’s Reform UK.

    Industry observers note that italy no longer seems to be immune to that trend. “We were convinced that the right stopped at Giorgia Meloni. Evidently, that was not the case,” said Mattia Diletti, a political scientist at Sapienza University of Rome. He compared National Future to the AfD due to the “strong value placed on national identity and national culture, as well as its strongly anti-European spirit.”.

    It has been revealed that much of Vannacci’s platform echoes nationalist-populist positions espoused by Meloni and her allies before she came to power. He explicitly endorses “remigration”—the large-scale deportation of migrants and asylum-seekers as well as long-term residents and those born in Europe but deemed “unassimilated.” Vannacci has described Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as an “existential war” for Russians, arguing that NATO’s eastward expansion forced it into a war.

    Industry observers note that just 10 years ago, Meloni openly cited the “great replacement” conspiracy theory. She called for an end to sanctions against Moscow as recently as February 2022, days before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. On the campaign trail that year, Meloni exploited anti-establishment sentiment and presented herself as an underdog, allowing her to build a base as the left wing fractured.

    However, the prime minister has governed as a more moderate leader than expected. Since taking office, Meloni has insisted to other European Union countries that she is no longer pro-Russia or Euroskeptic, embracing a pro-Ukraine stance and making several trips to Kyiv. She has maintained a cautious economic approach, focusing more on balancing the budget and adhering to European Commission procedures than on public investment.

    While Brussels appreciated this pivot, it was not welcomed by her whole base.

    “Meloni has become institutionalized, and many of her voters have not liked this,” stated Martina Carone, a pollster at Italy’s YouTrend. “People are struggling with rising petrol prices and the cost of living … it’s difficult to convince voters that things are getting better by presenting them with statistics.”.

    In a recent development, italy’s center-left, for its part, has struggled to overcome divisions between the Democratic Party and the populist Five-Star Movement over foreign policy, the environment, and the economy. Facing a fragmented opposition, Meloni long maintained enough support to avoid a serious challenge.

    Sources indicate that but she suffered a significant defeat in March, when voters rejected a constitutional reform proposed by her government. The emergence of Vannacci’s party, precisely as Meloni sought to project strength, is “exactly the kind of unexpected development that throws her plans into disarray,” stated Massimo Rebotti, a political journalist. Vannacci is borrowing from Meloni’s own opposition tactics: criticizing those in power without bearing any responsibility for governing.

    National Future surged in the polls in August and September before slumping more recently. But even on the margins, it could pose a threat to Meloni in next year’s general elections. Around two-thirds of Italy’s parliamentary seats are distributed proportionally in multimember districts; the remaining seats are filled in single-member districts using a first-past-the-post system. Meloni’s coalition is particularly vulnerable in these single-member constituencies.

    If the center-left wins enough of those districts, then Meloni’s current coalition could fail to win a parliamentary majority. Meloni could instead form an electoral alliance with National Future. But that would put her in a sticky position with European allies, who are wary of a party described by the Financial Times as “Russia’s ‘Trojan horse’ in Italy.”.

    Though there is no documented link between Vannacci and the Kremlin, the National Future leader has praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for restoring the country’s wealth and international standing. His foreign-policy platform aligns with that of Moscow: He opposes EU rearmament, wants to restore economic ties with Russia, and has called on Ukraine to accept Russian peace terms.

    According to recent reports, meloni has publicly ruled out allying with anyone who opposes support for Ukraine. After all, an alliance with Vannacci would erode the credibility that Meloni has built in Brussels as a fixture at meetings of the so-called “coalition of the willing,” with potentially significant financial consequences.

    Sources indicate that in June, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen signaled her openness to Meloni’s request for more budget flexibility, allocating 14 billion euros over three years to mitigate increasing energy costs. The arrangement relies on the EU’s national escape clause, which allows states to deviate from approved expenditure plans by up to 0.3 percent of GDP annually due to exceptional circumstances.

    Created to accommodate increased defense spending amid the war in Ukraine, the clause has been extended to account for energy security as well. The EU also quietly let Italy off the hook when it overshot its debt-to-GDP ratio last year above the bloc’s fiscal ceiling. If Meloni were to let Vannacci—who opposes the EU rearmament plan—into her coalition, these concessions would likely be impossible for Brussels to justify.

    In October, facing a threat from Vannacci’s party, Meloni’s coalition pushed through an electoral law that scraps most of the single-member constituencies ahead of next year’s elections. The upcoming law includes a bonus system to hand whichever coalition or electoral list that exceeds 42 percent of the vote 70 extra seats in the lower house and 35 extra seats in the Senate to reach a governing majority. If no coalition reaches that threshold, then seats are allocated proportionally.

    Meloni is also still shifting her policies to the right to connect with extreme factions within her base. In July, the prime minister proposed a law to make minors between the ages of 14 and 18 automatically presumed to be criminally liable. She has proposed a cap on foreign students in classrooms and a burqa ban.

    Sources indicate that the prime minister is also cautiously recalibrating her stance on Ukraine. At the beginning of her term, Meloni made political and military support for Kyiv an unequivocal objective of her foreign policy. At the time, more than half of Italians were willing to back Ukraine. As that support began to wane, Meloni could still afford to prioritize her standing with allies abroad over potential discontent at home, given that there was no opposition capable of unseating her.

    Industry observers note that now, however, Meloni talks about Ukraine as little as possible. Only 28 percent of Italians support arming Ukraine today, according to an Ipsos poll; it is particularly unpopular among right-wing voters. According to Rebotti, aid to Ukraine is Vannacci’s matter to exploit, since his party “can call for the money being spent to be used in other ways, from healthcare to security to education.”.

    Sources indicate that in recent months, Meloni has remarked that she is opposed to providing Ukraine with more effective offensive weapons and expressed reservations about Kyiv joining the EU. She postponed the delivery of an aid package in August, disrupting an established six-month schedule. Meloni said the package would only contain power generators, but Italian media reports that it included weapons.

    Industry observers note that italy’s bilateral aid to Ukraine has always been modest, amounting to just 0.24 percent of its GDP, which places it 18th of 27 EU countries. The risk is more symbolic: A founding member of both the Group of Seven and the EU cutting back its assistance to Kyiv would weaken the narrative of unity that the EU has built up as U.S. President Donald Trump has scaled back aid to Ukraine. It would also give a boost to pro-Russian parties across Europe that hope for similar pullbacks.

    Recent findings suggest that to win in 2027, Meloni must solve a nearly impossible equation. Allying with Vannacci could guarantee a majority but cost her major international support. Refusing that alliance could split the right-wing vote, either costing her power or producing a hung parliament and leaving Meloni dependent on the center-left. The question is whether Meloni’s rightward shift will be enough to navigate that narrow path.

    Giorgio Ghiglione is a freelance writer in Milan. His work has appeared in the Guardian, Al Jazeera, and Internazionale. X: @giorgioghiglion.

    #145326. A Upcoming Kind of Foreign Agent

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3109 w)

    A Upcoming Kind of Foreign Agent

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.
    • Foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding.
    • Recent findings suggest that like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.

    Foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding. President George Washington warned in his Farewell Address that “foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government.” The old methods have certainly not gone out of vogue; just this week Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. But today, a new type of foreign agent has arrived: Chinese artificial intelligence companies.

    Recent findings suggest that like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use. But their makers train them to promote the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). American businesses are outsourcing more and more critical decisions to AI. If Washington does nothing, those businesses will hand over control to models whose objective is to promote a foreign government.

    Recent findings suggest that although U.S. policymakers now debate banning Chinese AI, the tried-and-true American solution is not censorship but disclosure. In 1938, Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Rather than outlaw propaganda, FARA allowed foreign agents to continue spreading it—as long as they registered with the government and disclosed whom they really worked for. Their communications also had to carry a conspicuous label naming their foreign sponsor.

    Sources indicate that FARA’s wisdom has aged well over the decades. In recent years, the Justice Department has ordered the Russian state television network RT and the Chinese state media organizations Xinhua and CGTN to register as foreign agents and to label their content as such. Those who failed to register as foreign agents, such as Paul Manafort, President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign chairman, and former U.S. Representative David Rivera of Florida, were sentenced to prison. (Trump pardoned Manafort in 2020.).

    Today, rather than banning AI companies controlled by foreign governments, the United States should treat them as foreign agents under FARA. No newly introduced statute is needed. Washington should simply enforce the one on the books. Of course, FARA is no silver bullet against all foreign influence, but it fits the shape of this problem. A handful of known Chinese companies, such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, build the models that American businesses increasingly let think and act for them. The Justice Department can reach every one of them.

    Recent findings suggest that democracy is strong enough to survive foreign influence but not invisible foreign influence. And to make sure the world does not subordinate its decision-making to Beijing, Washington and its allies must create an allied AI compact and then spread their own models far and wide.

    Recent findings suggest that american AI models, such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, are under no obligation to promote the U.S. government’s message. Ask Claude about Trump’s and President Joe Biden’s biggest failures or about the United States’ darkest chapters, and it will answer. Not so for Chinese AI models. When I asked the Chinese chatbot DeepSeek to “tell me about the CCP” in November, it answered that the party “is the vanguard of the Chinese working class, the Chinese people, and the Chinese nation. . . . The Party’s leadership is the most essential characteristic of socialism with Chinese characteristics and is the fundamental guarantee for China’s development and progress.” Such boosterish language appears by design.

    According to recent reports, by law, Chinese AI models must never go against the Chinese government. Under the country’s 2023 regulations on generative AI, they must “uphold the Core Socialist Values” and may not engage in “harming the nation’s image” or “undermining national unity and social stability.” The Chinese government released a technical standard that laid out what these high-level declarations mean in practice: AI developers should have a list of at least 10,000 banned keywords, and their models must refuse to answer at least 95 percent of test questions the CCP finds objectionable. Developers must also scrub their training data of any history Beijing does not like. In short, the models must act as card-carrying members of the CCP.

    That is why, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s AI evaluators found in 2025, DeepSeek pushes Chinese propaganda at far higher rates than American models do, even when run on American servers. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service found that DeepSeek inserted praise of the Chinese state unprompted, and it concluded that China uses DeepSeek to instill “a distorted, self-serving world view in the Western information space.”.

    Industry observers note that but these models are not just propaganda parrots—they are taught to “think” about how to promote Beijing’s perspective. Ask an AI model something complex, and it will “reason” for a while. As it thinks, it produces an internal monologue called its chain of thought. Users rarely see it. There, it decides which facts are relevant and which to discard, what advice to give, and what autonomous actions to take. Silicon Valley is terrified that these chains of thought will become corrupt—that models will start scheming and lying, becoming “misaligned.” But a different kind of corruption is already here.

    In a recent development, although American models’ chains of thought usually focus on helping the user, China’s do something else: prioritize the party line. When researchers funded by Sweden’s Psychological Defense Agency looked at how Qwen, Alibaba’s flagship model, reasons about China, they found an internal checklist to keep the answer positive, avoid criticism, and focus on achievements. So when an American company asks a question on which Beijing has a view, a Chinese model may discard all evidence that points the other way. As the world delegates more research, writing, and decision-making to Chinese AI models, it risks infusing the CCP’s goals into every action taken.

    Sources indicate that these models are also highly persuasive. In a study published last year in Nature, researchers had some 6,000 voters in the United States, Canada, and Poland chat with AI models that argued for a candidate. The study found that a single conversation shifted the preferences of opposition voters in Canada and Poland by about ten percentage points. AI persuades by flooding a user with confident and authoritative-sounding facts—statistics, historical claims, and the like.

    Sources indicate that chinese AI models also exhibit strange behaviors beyond the spreading of propaganda. In October, the Canadian AI firm Cohere reported that during a security test, Alibaba’s Qwen tried to upload a file to a cloud server in Beijing, completely unprompted. The behavior was rare for Qwen, only observed once in testing, and Cohere said it could not tell whether it was “deliberate or a leftover glitch from training.” A study by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike found that when customers asked DeepSeek to write code that mentions groups Beijing finds politically “sensitive,” such as Tibetans, Uyghurs, or the religious movement Falun Gong, the model became up to 50 percent more likely to write code with severe security flaws. CrowdStrike suggested that one possible cause is China’s rule that models adhere to “core socialist values.”.

    Industry observers note that despite these findings, Chinese AI is enormously popular. Last year, downloads of Chinese open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download from the Internet and run on their own hardware—surpassed those of American ones across the world. Developers have built more than 150,000 models on Alibaba’s Qwen alone. By September 2026, Chinese models handled up to 67 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a popular AI marketplace, up from around ten percent in February.

    According to recent reports, american companies have embraced them. In March, a user discovered that Cursor, a popular coding tool, had built its fresh model by retraining Kimi, a model from the Chinese manufacturer Moonshot AI. Airbnb, DoorDash, and the legal-services AI company Harvey use Chinese models as well. Many others likely do, too, in secret. The models are spreading even faster abroad, from Germany’s Siemens to Singapore’s national AI program to startups in Africa. The reason is simple economics: Chinese models are very cheap and very good.

    Although most American AI companies do not release open-weight models, most Chinese companies do. So an American firm must pay Anthropic for each use of its unmodifiable models, but it can download Kimi for free, retrain it however it wants, and pay only for the electricity and chips to run it. Kimi also runs on a firm’s own servers, whereas Claude runs on Anthropic’s. Even if a firm uses the most expensive DeepSeek model run on DeepSeek’s servers, it can produce the same amount of text as Anthropic’s top models at one-20th the cost.

    In terms of capabilities, the research group Epoch AI judges Chinese models to be only about seven months behind American ones. For the price, they get the job done. And Chinese companies are now building agentic AI systems to compete with Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. In October, DeepSeek released an open-source prototype of its “Super-Agent” system.

    It has been revealed that although AI is a new technology, Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI fit FARA’s text and history. The statute applies when a foreign principal is identified; in the case of Chinese AI models, it is the Chinese government and the CCP. The Justice Department would also have to show that the Chinese AI company acts “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of the principal. Chinese AI companies would qualify because they must promote CCP viewpoints and cooperate with the state’s intelligence agencies. They also receive subsidies, and party organizations are embedded in each company. This is the difference between Chinese AI and other foreign AI. For example, France’s public investment bank has a stake in the French AI company Mistral, but no French law requires Mistral to build its models to serve the French government.

    In a recent development, beijing will surely respond that Washington, too, has tried to control American AI companies, such as through Trump’s July 2025 executive order against “woke AI.” But that order affects only what federal agencies can procure, and a company can opt out of being a federal contractor. Meanwhile, Chinese law forces Chinese AI companies to train their models to “support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts.”.

    It has been revealed that for FARA to apply, the agent must engage in certain activities, such as attempting to influence Americans or publishing content. Chinese AI companies do both by distributing models that spread propaganda. The statute exempts purely commercial activity, but only if it is “private and nonpolitical” and does not directly promote a foreign government’s political interests. Chinese AI models engage in political speech on a government’s behalf, and the Justice Department has denied the exemption to agents of foreign governments.

    Industry observers note that after registration, the genius of the statute can kick in. Chinese AI companies must disclose extensive information to the U.S. government: their funding sources, their written contracts and oral agreements, and the influence activities they undertake. Those that fail to register or omit information face both civil and criminal penalties.

    All content they disseminate must also bear a foreign-agent label: “a conspicuous statement,” in the statute’s words. The Justice Department sets the rules for what that looks like, and it has not updated them since 2003. In January 2025, the Justice Department proposed amendments to these rules to revision them for the digital age. The proposed amendments would require a label on “each individual post” online, such as on social media platforms, but they do not address AI foreign agents. The final rule should require every message from DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen to carry the disclaimer: “This was generated by an agent of the Chinese government and Chinese Communist Party.”.

    Industry observers note that the standard objection is that ordinary citizens do not read disclosures. That may be true of long medical forms or Securities and Exchange Commission filings, but this label would be short. And disclosure works because experts—investors, journalists, researchers—read filings and react. When researchers and lawmakers flagged gaps in China Daily’s FARA filings, the Chinese media company disclosed that it had paid millions of dollars to The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to publish its propaganda. Payments to the Journal ended that same month. Forcing Chinese AI companies to register under FARA would also shed light on how far Chinese AI is spreading so that Americans can decide, with real data, whether they want further action, such as a ban.

    American companies that use Chinese AI models can also become foreign agents if they fall under a foreign principal’s “direction or control” and engage in activities subject to FARA. This could happen in two ways: the tech giant serves as a “CCP spokesperson,” or as a “CCP executive.”.

    In the first, an American firm takes an unmodified Chinese AI model and lets Americans discuss political problems with it—say, via a video game character or a customer service chatbot. The model returns its usual propaganda, so the company has effectively hired a CCP spokesperson. Accordingly, it must label its outputs. Both the Justice Department and a federal court have found that rebroadcasting unmodified programming from the Russian state outlet Sputnik turns an American company into a foreign agent. Of course, American companies can avoid FARA obligations if they do not engage in any of the activities listed by the statute, such as discussing politics. A company whose public-facing Chinese AI model discusses only, say, hotel check-in times, not politics, would not be a CCP spokesperson.

    In the second scenario, an American company outsources so much of its decision-making to an unmodified Chinese AI model that it has effectively hired a CCP executive. If a company hired a brilliant human strategist who always pushed Beijing’s interests, and the company followed that advice, FARA would apply. The same logic holds if an American company cedes control to the Chinese government by giving Beijing’s models high decision-making authority. Although it may sound fantastical, 64 percent of chief executives surveyed in IBM’s 2026 CEO Study say they already feel comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI input; overall, CEOs expect AI to make 48 percent of routine operational decisions autonomously by 2030. An American company that wants to avoid becoming a CCP executive must be sure not to fall under the direction or control of such models. The Justice Department should update its 2020 guidance on what constitutes “direction or control,” spelling out how much decision-making a company can outsource to AI before it has effectively hired a “CCP executive.”.

    In a recent development, american companies could attempt to train away the party bias in the Chinese AI models they adopt, but it is unclear whether that is even possible. Perplexity, an American AI manufacturer, trained DeepSeek to stop ignoring questions about the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and about human rights abuses in Xinjiang, but that does not fix the deeper problem of corrupt chains of thought. As these models get more capable, Chinese AI companies may also find cleverer ways to hide instructions. Or they could just stick them in the contract: some recent DeepSeek licenses prohibit modifying models to generate “inappropriate content” under Chinese law, making propaganda part of the deal. If research highlights that companies can reliably remove the bias, the Justice Department and the Commerce Department should concern standards on how to train away FARA liability.

    Although Pam Bondi, then the U.S. attorney general, limited criminal FARA charges in 2025 to “conduct similar to more traditional espionage by foreign government actors,” Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Justice Department indicates it is considering a new rule to “keep pace with technological change.” It should include AI foreign agents.

    Of course, Washington should wield FARA’s expansive authorities with care. Frivolous prosecutions under the statute could stifle democracy. Other countries have used foreign-agent laws to shut down civil society. Since 2022, Russia has barred anyone it deems a foreign agent from holding office and organizing public events. Still, FARA is a far narrower statute, and it should stay that way. It reaches only those acting under the direction or control of a foreign principal, and it simply requires registration and labeling, leaving the speaker free to keep speaking. Chinese AI companies that are required by law to promote the CCP’s interests fit squarely within what Congress had in mind when it approved FARA in 1938.

    In a recent development, FARA can help in the United States, but the problem is global. Chinese AI is spreading rapidly in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. That is no accident. In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping unveiled the World AI Cooperation Organization, a Shanghai-based group of 29 countries meant to make AI “beneficial, safe, and fair,” along with a development initiative to export Chinese AI worldwide. The United States and its allies cannot allow CCP executives and spokespeople to run the world’s companies and governments.

    Unfortunately, the American alternatives are not particularly attractive. The most capable U.S. models are far more expensive, are largely unmodifiable, and may contain their own biases. That is why the United States and its allies should create an AI compact rooted in transparency, with standards that make countries comfortable adopting allied models as their own. These should include freedom from state ideological mandates, disclosure of how the models were trained to be helpful and safe, and independent auditing.

    In a recent development, every member of such a compact should also adopt FARA’s wisdom by mandating labels on government-directed AI, and the United States should hold American AI companies to those transparency standards. The bloc should then release models that match China’s in price and quality (that is, around seven months behind the American frontier). Allied governments can help pay for computing power and electricity, assist in clearing regulatory hurdles, and make bulk purchase commitments to bring prices down. American companies may cut prices on their older models on their own to compete with Chinese models. If they do not, lower prices for those worse models should be the condition for the public support they receive, such as federal contracts and permission to lease federal land for data centers, just as a pharmaceutical manufacturer can charge high prices for only a set period before generic drugs arrive. The compact’s members should also use export loans and guarantees to steer developing countries toward allied AI.

    By welcoming supposedly free technology from China, the United States and its allies have unwittingly invited countless foreign agents to their shores. The Foreign Agents Registration Act can strip away the disguise, and an allied AI compact can give the world a better offer.

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.
