    #145311. The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2678 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
    • President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China.
    • It has been revealed that these worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

    In just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been announced, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”.

    It has been revealed that these worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting might ultimately yield little progress on major issues.

    Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

    If he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core issues that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

    Industry observers note that I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a upcoming concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

    But the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, are willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and are ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

    Sources indicate that yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

    Sources indicate that if they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious blueprint for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

    Lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they might be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Pyongyang and Seoul. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a initiative for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

    Recent findings suggest that the prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a fresh round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

    A summit offers Trump the opportunity to change course and try to convince Xi to restrain Putin. Trump has vowed to bring the war in Ukraine to an end, and the Chinese leader can help him achieve that goal. Xi has enormous leverage over Putin: China backs the Kremlin diplomatically, is the largest buyer of Russian oil and gas, and is the main supplier of dual-use items such as semiconductors and machine tools that are critical to Russian weapons manufacturing.

    Xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi could advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

    Trump and Xi could press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, might convince Putin to relent on at least some of these issues.

    Recent findings suggest that trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to glitch maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

    Sources indicate that neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

    Sources indicate that as a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

    Xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop or at least slow the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

    Recent findings suggest that xi could also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf, release frozen Iranian assets, and remove economic sanctions. Washington might well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiations toward a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi could help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

    Beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Xi and Putin. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, New START, ended in February. There are at the moment no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

    In October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon has projected that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it in nearly the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

    Realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

    According to recent reports, trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area in which cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Gaza or Yemen. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

    Recent findings suggest that yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force on Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a new Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

    Industry observers note that trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

    Sources indicate that A summit next week will not usher in a fresh era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It might not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump would begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.

    This month, Nextnova celebrated the official inauguration of its new solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City, marking an notable milestone in strengthening America’s domestic solar manufacturing industry.

    The facility will manufacture high-efficiency solar cells using advanced automation, Industry 4.0 technologies, and comprehensive digital traceability.

    Production is scheduled to begin in March 2027 with an initial annual capacity of 2 GW, designed to expand to 5 GW as market demand grows.

    According to recent reports, nextnova celebrates the inauguration of its newly introduced solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City. Credit: Nextnova.

    Designed for maximum quality and reliability, the facility features fully integrated manufacturing execution systems (MES), automated inspection technologies, advanced process control, and a dedicated analytical laboratory supporting continuous quality verification throughout production.

    It has been revealed that nextnova notes that its commitment to transparent sourcing, manufacturing excellence, and scalable production provides customers with high-performance solar cells that support the continued growth of a secure and competitive U.S. solar industry.

    ICJ Finds Myanmar Committed Genocide. What Comes Next?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state.
    • Nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide.
    • In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state. Within just three months, security forces had killed thousands of people, razed hundreds of villages, committed widespread sexual violence, and forced some 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

    Nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide. The landmark ruling, delivered Thursday, marked the first time that the United Nations’ top court has found a country directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

    In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state. Within just three months, security forces had killed thousands of people, razed hundreds of villages, committed widespread sexual violence, and forced some 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

    Nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide. The landmark ruling, delivered Thursday, marked the first time that the United Nations’ top court has found a country directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

    Foreign Policy spoke with Tom Andrews, the former U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in Myanmar, a few hours after the ruling came down. He discussed the decision’s implications, including where justice lies for the world’s largest stateless population and how the ruling could affect similar genocide cases linked to the wars in Gaza and Ukraine.

    This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

    Foreign Policy: Earlier today, the ICJ found that Myanmar’s security forces had committed genocide against the country’s minority Rohingya Muslim community. For those who aren’t aware of the case, could you give a brief primer on the court’s findings?

    It has been revealed that tom Andrews: They were very explicit in their findings. They talked about the thousands and thousands of people who were killed, the thousands of women who were raped, the more than 2,000 children who were killed, the hundreds of thousands of homes that were burned.

    Industry observers note that I was in Bangladesh when people had arrived [in 2017], and I sat and talked to many people who had literally been running for their lives. And the stories they told me were just absolutely incredible. I mean the horror, the brutality, the systematic nature of the killing, of the rapes, of the torture, was just absolutely extraordinary. And, of course, more than 700,000 people escaped into Bangladesh; we know that 1.3 million are now in Bangladesh, in the largest refugee camp in the world.

    But what [the Rohingya] did was they pushed for justice and they pushed for accountability. And there were people who were victimized by this brutality, who came to the court, the International Court of Justice, and provided their own personal testimony, told their own stories in a private session, which I believe was a very powerful, powerful part of this whole process, where it allowed the judges to focus on the actual consequences, the human element of this.

    FP: This is the first time that the U.N.’s top court has found a nation directly responsible for genocide. What is the significance of that ruling?

    TA: History was made today. The standard for genocide is very, very high. And that is a reason why this is so remarkable. This is the first time it’s ever been made, because the standard not only includes the acts but also the intention behind those acts—that [the state] designed to harm a population in whole or in part.

    But the question that it begs is, well, OK, now what? Now that we’ve established genocide, are there consequences for genocide, and what are they? And the court has ruled that the regime in Myanmar is responsible for providing relief and compensation for the victims.

    I believe that that needs to occur both within the United Nations and outside of the United Nations. Within the United Nations, I believe that the United Nations Security Council should take this up. I think they should pass a resolution. I think that these individuals who were responsible for this genocide should be criminally prosecuted, and so there should be a reference to the International Criminal Court for that criminal prosecution.

    According to recent reports, I think it’s also notable for us to recognize that the killings that continue to go on are happening because the military junta—the generals and [junta leader] Min Aung Hlaing—has access to sophisticated weapons of war that it’s using to attack civilians. I think it’s really important that the international community do everything that it can to cut off that access to those weapons and those weapon materials, and the financing that’s being used to acquire those weapons and those weapon materials, so that we can stop that flow.

    Sources indicate that another step that they can take is to reject this rehabilitation campaign that Min Aung Hlaing has been involved in now for the past few months. He’s been traveling to states in the region, to his neighbors, to ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] states. He’s been invited into these capitals, welcomed into these capitals. He’s been seeking to gain greater acceptance within ASEAN and the structure of ASEAN. And I think what’s really vital is for those member states who have been moving in that direction of accepting or softening their relationship to Min Aung Hlaing and this genocidal regime to reverse those steps and that the regime be as isolated diplomatically as it deserves to be.

    FP: Do you think that the ruling will be enough, though, to actually push member states to take that next step and start to reverse the junta’s efforts to cast off its diplomatic pariah status?

    TA: I certainly hope so. I mean, this is unprecedented. This is a powerful, powerful moment for the world. I think it’s incredibly notable for the world to respond to that finding in a responsible way and that member states and their citizens need to stand up and make their voices very, very clear and very strong that their government needs to do everything that it can to isolate this regime, weaken this regime, take away this regime’s capacity to continue to commit murder against its own people.

    I mean, this is a moral imperative, and it is a call for everyone to make a moral stand for not only the Rohingya, not only for the people of Myanmar, but for justice and humanity around the world. Because the thing is, if we establish that there is no consequence for genocide, then we can be guaranteed that genocide is going to happen again. And it’s only by imposing consequences that we can begin to see justice prevail, not only in this case but in future cases.

    FP: What’s next for the Rohingya community themselves? The ICJ doesn’t have an enforcement mechanism, but could this case have a tangible impact on the future of that population?

    Industry observers note that TA: It can, and it should. First of all, the world has turned its back on the Rohingya. Support for the conditions in which they’re living, the refugee camps, has been declining. There have been increased difficulties in just being able to survive in these camps, in part, certainly, by the fact of the international community reversing commitments that it had made and support that it provided to people who are in these conditions for no fault of their own.

    Now, I think, with respect to reparations, the idea that the government of Myanmar—the current illegitimate regime of Myanmar—would accept the order of the court to provide compensation is, at best, a very, very remote possibility. In fact, I think that the chances of this happening are exactly zero. So, until there is a fresh regime that actually is legitimate and believes in justice and accountability and human rights, until that day happens, I think the world has to step forward, and I think there are options the world can take.

    It has been revealed that for example, the United Nations can establish a reparations fund and a mechanism to manage that. The United States, for example, seized over a billion dollars in assets from this regime. And that billion dollars can be used as part of a compensation fund, and that can then be built upon with governments coming forward to provide additional resources so that there is some form of justice and compensation for those who were victimized by these attacks.

    FP: What is the view coming out of Myanmar right now? Is there talk of this case possibly leading to something like regime change?

    TA: I’ve heard reports of additional hate speech that’s beginning to be drummed up, some of the nationalists that have used hate speech against the Rohingya in the past, that they are beginning to once again generate that kind of hatred against the Rohingya. It’s a dangerous moment in the country.

    FP: Obviously, this case has an outsized impact on Myanmar’s future, but could this ruling affect similar cases at the ICJ on the conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine?

    TA: It remains to be seen. The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations [Mike Waltz] posted a tweet in which—I’m paraphrasing here, but [he] accused the court of being poised to lower the standard for genocide, which could have an impact on future cases. And what’s happened is that the court was very explicit in saying that they used the current standard for genocide, including the standard of genocidal intent, in making this judgment. So, in fact, there was no lowering of the standard for genocide that some have accused the court of preparing to do.

    Recent findings suggest that I think what’s important is to focus on this case, to focus on this community and on people who were wronged, and to focus on our responsibility to them and to accountability and justice for them and to make sure that there is a consequence for genocide. So I’m hoping that we’re not distracted by what might happen in the future, that we’re focused on what’s happening right now.

    I saw a report that a child is killed in these attacks every 29 hours in Myanmar now. So, yes, we need to stop the atrocities from continuing, but we need to focus on responsibility and accountability for these acts and these acts of genocide.

    It has been revealed that alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp.

    #145305. The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3971 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
    • At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
    • Industry observers note that nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

    At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

    Industry observers note that nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

    Industry observers note that yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

    In recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

    At the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

    Recent findings suggest that the success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

    International efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

    In the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

    Today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

    According to recent reports, worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

    Industry observers note that there is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

    A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France confirmed the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

    Simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

    It has been revealed that the integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

    In a recent development, together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will rapidly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

    Political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

    Industry observers note that in this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

    It has been revealed that but these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

    Wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

    War also creates new dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

    Finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to upcoming waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

    According to recent reports, the world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

    In a recent development, but it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

    Recent findings suggest that spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

    Industry observers note that from day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

    Deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

    Countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

    Investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

    In a recent development, yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

    Reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

    Some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

    It has been revealed that other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

    The twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

    It has been revealed that all of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

    Sources indicate that strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

    The first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An revision to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly important, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The new seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats currently occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

    It has been revealed that permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

    Recent findings suggest that A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

    Industry observers note that another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral New START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

    Recent findings suggest that yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

    Industry observers note that technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

    It has been revealed that the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

    Industry observers note that proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a latest UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

    In a recent development, halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

    International financial institutions must be able to deliver financing quickly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

    Sources indicate that this is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, launched with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

    In a recent development, A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

    #145302. Latest Update: What the Yalta Comparison Really Reveals About Shenzhen

    Latest Update: What the Yalta Comparison Really Reveals About Shenzhen

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The moment that the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, was planned, commentators began comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference.
    • Industry observers note that the Kremlin was right about the symbolism, not least because this week’s summit produced little else.
    • Recent findings suggest that the moment that the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, was planned, commentators began comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    The moment that the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, was planned, commentators began comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference. Unsurprisingly, this narrative was particularly fueled by Moscow, where the British-Soviet-U.S. “Big Three” summit stands for the codification of Soviet control over half of Europe. Pyotr Tolstoy, the head of the foreign affairs committee in the Russian parliament, called the summit a “newly introduced Yalta.” Ultranationalist ideologue Alexander Dugin found the meeting “deeply symbolic,” while the Kremlin boasted that “the significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”.

    Industry observers note that the Kremlin was right about the symbolism, not least because this week’s summit produced little else. The joint “Declaration Toward Peace” adopted by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin says practically nothing. It pledges United Nations reform without specifics, future fuel shipments without volumes or deadlines, and a dialogue on nuclear risks without a clear path forward. Its most pointed passage is a warning to the International Criminal Court not to abuse its jurisdiction.

    Recent findings suggest that the moment that the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, was planned, commentators began comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference. Unsurprisingly, this narrative was particularly fueled by Moscow, where the British-Soviet-U.S. “Massive Three” summit stands for the codification of Soviet control over half of Europe. Pyotr Tolstoy, the head of the foreign affairs committee in the Russian parliament, called the summit a “new Yalta.” Ultranationalist ideologue Alexander Dugin found the meeting “deeply symbolic,” while the Kremlin boasted that “the significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”.

    The Kremlin was right about the symbolism, not least because this week’s summit produced little else. The joint “Declaration Toward Peace” adopted by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin says practically nothing. It pledges United Nations reform without specifics, future fuel shipments without volumes or deadlines, and a dialogue on nuclear risks without a clear path forward. Its most pointed passage is a warning to the International Criminal Court not to abuse its jurisdiction.

    Sources indicate that nothing about this is surprising. The vagueness on arms control reflects China’s lack of interest in it amid a rapid build-out of its nuclear forces. Ukraine is not mentioned, because Russia has made it repeatedly clear that it is not ready for peace in Europe on anything but its maximalist demands. Iran, too, was absent from the agenda, given Russian and Chinese support for Iran and the embarrassing cul-de-sac that the war represents for Trump.

    According to recent reports, but substance was hardly the point. The mere image of the three leaders sitting together made the summit significant—and made capitals from Taipei to Kyiv to Tokyo nervous that the three might strike a private understanding over their heads.

    To understand what yesterday’s summit really meant, Yalta is indeed a useful comparison—but mainly for the differences that it reveals.

    Sources indicate that the first is the diminished stature of today’s threesome. The Significant Three met as the victors of a war that had left much of Europe and Asia in ruins. What they decided at Yalta—and at the Potsdam Conference a few months later—drew lines that would last for more than four decades. The three leaders who met in Shenzhen are weak, each in his own way, and each of them needed a photo-op to project a strength that he does not fully possess.

    According to recent reports, china was not invited to Yalta because it was on the menu: U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin agreed on Soviet rights over the Manchurian railways and ports of Dairen and Port Arthur without consulting the Republic of China’s leader, Chiang Kai-shek.

    Eighty-one years later, a different China was the host. The location was carefully chosen: In 1980, when it became China’s first special economic zone, Shenzhen was a small town across the border from Hong Kong, whereas today it is one of the world’s leading technology and manufacturing hubs. But the rise that Shenzhen embodies is losing pace. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects Chinese economic growth to slow to 4.5 percent this year and 4 percent in 2027 as weak domestic demand and a real estate crisis weigh on the economy. Demographic decline will shrink the country’s population by 786 million by 2100. The flashy summit was also a way to distract the world from the change in China’s trajectory.

    Sources indicate that for Putin, the gain of face was even greater, given that by any material measure, Russia plays in a much smaller league. The IMF projects the U.S. GDP at $32.6 trillion in 2026 and China’s at $21.5 trillion. Russia’s is only about $2.7 trillion, roughly the size of Italy’s. Military spending tells the same story. In 2025, the United States spent $954 billion, China an estimated $336 billion, and Russia $190 billion. European NATO members together spent $559 billion, almost three times as much as Russia.

    Putin’s seat in Shenzhen was therefore the dividend of nearly two decades of growing, calculated aggressiveness. Georgia, Syria, the 2014 and 2022 invasions of Ukraine, and the current hybrid attacks across Europe are a sequence of moves resting on the same bet. Moscow has converted Europe’s passivity into status, compensating for what it lacks in economic and military weight with a willingness to use force that none of its rivals share.

    It has been revealed that the bet paid off because Europe preferred to ignore the implications. Germany shrugged off Russia’s 2014 invasion of Crimea and the Donbas and moved forward with Nord Stream 2, thereby entrenching the continent’s energy dependence on Moscow. Since 2022, Europe has financed Ukraine’s defense without ever resolving to push for Kyiv’s victory. And Washington bears its share in encouraging Putin, from former President Barack Obama’s impotent red line in Syria in 2013 to Trump granting Moscow sanctions relief and a seat among the great powers before any settlement of Russia’s war.

    Industry observers note that for Trump, the summit was a welcome respite from a string of setbacks. On Nov. 3, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, winning various Republican strongholds for the first time in generations. The botched attack on Iran contributed to this electoral punishment, not least through its impact on gas prices.

    Add to this that Trump has never hidden his admiration for leaders who govern without democratic constraints. A seat at the table with two of them, with all the ceremony that came with it, was worth a great deal to a president facing a hostile Congress and having few foreign successes to show for the year. “It’s a massive win for us,” he told reporters as the meeting opened.

    The strategic environment could hardly be more different from 1945. The leaders who met then were looking to consolidate the status quo that had emerged from the war, which they all found acceptable. By contrast, the three powers that met in Shenzhen are, each in its own way, fundamentally revisionist.

    According to recent reports, china has its sights on Taiwan and wresting technological leadership from the United States. Russia has its war in Europe and a relationship with Beijing that becomes more lopsided every year. The United States is renegotiating its alliances and trade policy while stuck in a quagmire in Iran. The U.S.-China trade truce expires in January, and the Nvidia scandal highlights how far the technology rivalry now reaches. All three are navigating a strategic environment in flux, which each sees as an intermediate stop to improve its own position.

    In a recent development, the third and deepest difference is vividly depicted by Europe’s absence. At Yalta, Europe sat among the victors. France, following four years under German occupation and the collaborationist Vichy regime, was of course not invited. For Poland and much of Central Europe, the conference is a reminder of a settlement imposed at its expense. But British Prime Minister Winston Churchill spoke for a European power that had fought the war since 1939—and the order that he helped design, from the postwar occupation of Germany to the creation of the United Nations, was one with freedom at its very core.

    In Shenzhen, no European leader was in the room, the visible outcome of decades of strategic decline. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a forum of 21 Pacific Rim economies of which no European Union member state is a member.

    In fact, each of the three leaders at the table is, in different ways, working against Europe. China does it through trade: In 2025, the EU ran a deficit of 359.8 billion euros with China; the largest category of imports was mechanical appliances, electrical machinery, and equipment, the industrial core that Europe is trying to protect.

    Russia does it through force: Its war against Ukraine is in its fifth year, and its hybrid campaign of sabotage, drone incursions, disinformation, and intimidation now reaches deep into EU territory.

    Sources indicate that the United States does it through ideological disdain, made crystal clear by Vice President J.D. Vance’s speech at the 2025 Munich Security Conference and by a National Security Strategy that warned of Europe’s “civilizational erasure” and committed Washington to supporting “patriotic” (read: far-right) parties on the continent, on top of tariffs on European goods at levels unseen in the postwar trans-Atlantic relationship.

    This genuinely anti-European stance was the only real common denominator in Shenzhen—a hostility fueled by Europe’s weakness, to be sure, but even more by a shared ideology of power. Yalta was a meeting of champions of different worldviews. Roosevelt and Churchill embodied the liberal democracies that were about to defeat Nazism. Stalin embodied a revolutionary state with a rival vision of political and economic order and ultimately of humanity itself. Within three years, this ideological divergence would harden into the Cold War. For all its ill effects on the nations caught on the Soviet side, Yalta is still an icon of pragmatism across an ideological divide.

    It has been revealed that shenzhen was the exact opposite. The three leaders do not lack conflicting interests. Washington wants Beijing in a trilateral arms control framework that the Chinese Foreign Ministry calls “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic.” The United States is at war with Iran, and the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz hits China’s energy supplies. Russia and China are far from strategic allies, and diplomatic protocol in Shenzhen revealed how unequal their relationship has become.

    Recent findings suggest that but on the question that divided the room at Yalta—namely, how power should be constrained and legitimized—the three leaders in Shenzhen are closer to one another than any of them is to almost every other leader across the world. All three think of sovereignty as the right of strong states to act without external constraint. All three read the world in terms of spheres of influence and privilege bilateral deals to multilateral rules.

    It has been revealed that finally, all three regard checks and balances, independent courts, and a free press as nuisances and obstacles at home and abroad. It is telling that one of the four points of their declaration—and the only one that wasn’t lukewarm boilerplate—defends the immunity of state officials and warns the International Criminal Court against abusing its jurisdiction.

    According to recent reports, in this sense, all three are anti-Western in the deepest sense of the term. For Xi and Putin, rejecting the underlying idea of the West is long-standing doctrine, but the United States—the country that once defined and defended the West—now shares much of the same inclination.

    Industry observers note that this is how the world has changed since 1945. At Yalta, ideological opposites negotiated a balance of power. In Shenzhen, three leaders with a shared worldview but competing interests discussed the affairs of the world, producing symbolism rather than substance. The two superpowers and their Russian sidekick were in a bubble, with neither the West nor anyone else represented in the room.

    For all the lack of substance, that may be the summit’s most important outcome: If what we saw this week portends a lasting realignment of the United States, this summit’s legacy could be far greater than the one to which it was so eagerly compared.

    #145301. Industry News: La última oportunidad para la paz
