    Industry News: La última oportunidad para la paz

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.
    • Recent findings suggest that en algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable.
    • Recent findings suggest that no hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.

    Cómo evitar otra guerra mundial.

    Recent findings suggest that en algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable. Las guerras de agresión, como las de Ucrania, el Líbano o Irán, aumentan y siembran horror, ruina y el temor a una confrontación global. Los gobiernos piensan cada vez más en la guerra como algo para lo que hay que prepararse y presupuestar. El gasto militar no deja de crecer, las carreras tecnológicas y armamentísticas se intensifican, y cada vez más países se plantean si deberían dotarse de un arsenal nuclear disuasorio que garantice su seguridad.

    Recent findings suggest that no hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra. Supone regresar a una norma que imperó durante la mayor parte de la historia de la humanidad. La guerra era el eje vertebrador del sistema internacional. Era la vía natural por la que los Estados zanjaban sus disputas o ensanchaban su territorio a costa de vecinos más débiles.

    Pero la inmensa devastación que produjeron las dos guerras mundiales en la primera mitad del siglo XX hizo inaceptable ese statu quo. Los países se unieron en un empeño común: que la guerra dejara de ser un instrumento legítimo de la política de Estado y pasara a ser un acto ilegal. Las guerras no terminaron en 1945, pero durante años la comunidad internacional las condenó de forma abrumadora.

    En las últimas décadas, sin embargo, el compromiso de los gobiernos con la causa de la paz se ha debilitado. En 2003, millones de personas salieron a las calles en cientos de ciudades para oponerse a la invasión de Irak liderada por Estados Unidos. Y, aun así, la guerra siguió adelante. Iniciada a partir de premisas falsas y en violación del derecho internacional, arrasó Irak, agravó la inestabilidad regional y avivó el resentimiento y el terrorismo contra los países occidentales. Aquel conflicto marcó, además, un punto de inflexión. Desde entonces, la búsqueda de la paz ha ido retrocediendo en la agenda internacional, arrinconada por la creciente competencia geopolítica y la desatención o la indiferencia hacia los esfuerzos multilaterales que durante décadas pusieron freno a la guerra.

    According to recent reports, este camino conduce a una nueva guerra mundial: la catástrofe que el orden del siglo XX se propuso evitar. Ante ese futuro sombrío en el horizonte, los gobiernos deben reaprender el arte de oponerse a la guerra. Todos los países, incluido el mío, España, tienen la responsabilidad de actuar para limitar la capacidad de otros de librar la guerra y para fortalecer las instituciones internacionales que han de ser garantes de la paz.

    Recent findings suggest that el éxito de este proyecto dependerá de un multilateralismo expansivo, al que yo llamo «maxilateralismo»: una cooperación que abarque al mayor número posible de países, en lugar de limitarse a pequeñas coaliciones ad hoc. Su ambición es que la guerra resulte cada vez más inviable, incluso inimaginable. En 2003, manifestantes por toda España coreaban «¡No a la guerra!». En 2026, el mundo no puede volver a ignorarlos.

    Los esfuerzos internacionales por desterrar la guerra como instrumento de política nacional se remontan al Pacto Briand-Kellogg de 1928, un tratado firmado en París por 15 países, al que posteriormente se sumaron decenas más. No bastó para impedir la Segunda Guerra Mundial, pero plantó una semilla. Cuando representantes de 50 países se reunieron en San Francisco en 1945 para crear las Naciones Unidas, recuperaron el espíritu y los principios del Pacto y añadieron lo que había faltado: estructura institucional. La Carta de Naciones Unidas prohibió recurrir a la amenaza o al uso de la fuerza contra la integridad territorial o la independencia política de otro Estado. Y, a diferencia de su predecesor de 1928, respaldó esa prohibición con instituciones facultadas para hacerla cumplir.

    According to recent reports, en las décadas siguientes, estas instituciones levantaron un orden que castigaba las violaciones al derecho internacional e incentivaba la cooperación y la diplomacia. Al mismo tiempo, el rechazo popular a la guerra y al militarismo de la Guerra Fría cobraba fuerza en todo el mundo. Se hizo visible en la resistencia a la guerra de Vietnam y en los movimientos de masas contra las armas nucleares. El pacifismo alcanzó su punto álgido en los años noventa, cuando una sociedad civil global pujante se movilizó en defensa de causas humanitarias y Naciones Unidas tenía autoridad para abanderar una ambiciosa agenda de paz.

    In a recent development, hoy, sin embargo, hay más conflictos armados que en ningún otro momento desde 1946. Según el Programa de Datos sobre Conflictos de Uppsala, en 2025 hubo 65 conflictos activos con participación estatal, el doble que en 2010. Se calcula que en estos conflictos murieron 250.000 personas: la cifra anual más alta desde el genocidio de Ruanda hace más de 30 años. Cerca de 120 millones de personas en todo el mundo siguen desplazadas por la guerra.

    Y lo más inquietante: las guerras de agresión, que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas, están de vuelta. Rusia invadió Ucrania. Estados Unidos e Israel atacaron Irán. Y mientras los combates se prolongan año tras año en lugares como el Líbano, Sudán o Yemen, resulta evidente que la guerra está siendo aceptada de nuevo como algo normal.

    Sources indicate that nada indica que esta tendencia vaya a frenarse. Los presupuestos militares se han disparado hasta niveles no vistos en generaciones, en detrimento del gasto social y de desarrollo. Solo en la última década, el gasto mundial en defensa ha aumentado más de un 40 %, y muchos países han duplicado sus presupuestos militares. Los casi 3 billones de dólares que el mundo destina cada año a defensa se acercan al producto interior bruto de todo el continente africano. Incluso países con una larga tradición de contención militar, como Alemania, Dinamarca, Japón y Noruega, se están rearmando a toda velocidad, y algunos están recuperando el servicio militar.

    Recent findings suggest that aún más estremecedor es el regreso de la amenaza de guerra nuclear. Los nueve Estados con armas nucleares están modernizando sus arsenales y aumentando su capacidad destructiva. Se calcula que el arsenal de China ha pasado de entre unas 200-300 cabezas nucleares a finales de la década de 2010 a 620 este año. Corea del Norte también ha ampliado el suyo, de entre 10-20 cabezas estimadas en 2018 a unas 60 este año, y ha desarrollado plataformas de lanzamiento cada vez más sofisticadas. En marzo, Francia anunció el primer aumento de su número de cabezas nucleares desde 1992. Estados Unidos y Rusia, las dos mayores potencias nucleares del mundo, no han sido capaces de preservar el último tratado que ponía límites a sus arsenales estratégicos. Y cada vez más potencias no nucleares han empezado a plantearse adquirir armas nucleares propias.

    Al mismo tiempo, la inteligencia artificial (IA) está dotando a la guerra de armas cada vez más peligrosas. La supervisión humana se reduce progresivamente a medida que la IA permite automatizar ciberataques contra redes eléctricas, hospitales y sistemas financieros. Hay sistemas de IA que ya han logrado infiltrarse en organismos públicos y han hecho posible la producción masiva de deepfakes y de campañas de desinformación.

    Industry observers note that la integración de la IA en las tecnologías nucleares es una amenaza existencial: al acelerar la toma de decisiones, comprime el tiempo disponible para el juicio humano. Del mismo modo, el uso de la IA en biotecnología podría rebajar drásticamente las barreras a la experimentación nociva y al desarrollo de armas biológicas. En ambos terrenos, esta tecnología está elevando a niveles sin precedentes el riesgo de errores de cálculo, de escaladas involuntarias y de destrucción masiva.

    En conjunto, estas dinámicas multiplican las probabilidades de que cualquier crisis desemboque rápidamente en la aniquilación del planeta. Por desgracia, los países están fabricando los instrumentos de la catástrofe a la velocidad vertiginosa de la innovación, mientras que los instrumentos de control avanzan al ritmo, mucho más lento, de la diplomacia.

    Los cambios políticos están alejando al mundo de la paz. Lo empujan hacia la militarización y la confrontación. Un mundo multipolar no es, por definición, más peligroso. Pero la erosión de las normas y de las instituciones que deberían encauzar las tensiones entre los distintos polos está provocando que el mundo se vuelva especialmente volátil. La competencia entre grandes potencias se intensifica: las ansias de hegemonía alientan políticas exteriores agresivas y los Estados revisionistas desafían las normas y las fronteras establecidas. El nacionalismo beligerante crece. Los movimientos de extrema derecha promueven una visión del mundo en la que las relaciones internacionales son un juego de suma cero y los países deben competir en lugar de cooperar. Incluso dirigentes de centro están adoptando la retórica de la guerra. Aunque no pretendan iniciar una, sus palabras abonan una mentalidad militarista peligrosa.

    In a recent development, en este clima de rivalidad, las guerras de agresión se envuelven en discursos de necesidad, liberación, legítima defensa o justicia histórica. Los agresores presentan sus operaciones como inevitables, después de haber demonizado a sus adversarios para justificar un ataque preventivo. Venden cada guerra como la respuesta a la inseguridad: la guerra que acabará con todas las guerras.

    Recent findings suggest that pero estas guerras no harán del mundo un lugar más seguro. Cada vez que un Estado desata una guerra de agresión, erosiona las normas que protegen a todos los países frente al uso arbitrario de la fuerza, incluido el propio Estado agresor.

    Las guerras tienen un coste inmenso. Destrozan sociedades y truncan vidas. En 2025, según los registros de Naciones Unidas, al menos un civil murió en conflicto armado cada 14 minutos, y más de cinco millones de personas se vieron obligadas a huir de sus países. El coste económico también es altísimo. La guerra que enfrenta a Estados Unidos e Israel con Irán ha alterado gravemente el comercio marítimo y el tráfico aéreo y ha disparado los precios de la energía, los fertilizantes y otras materias primas. Millones de personas en todo el mundo están sufriendo las consecuencias.

    Industry observers note that la guerra genera, además, nuevos peligros. Una vez que empiezan los combates, su rumbo es imprevisible. Los conflictos tienden a arrastrar a nuevos actores y a desbordarse hacia los países vecinos. La guerra de Irán vuelve a ser un ejemplo claro. Desde febrero de 2026, Irán ha atacado objetivos en varios países del Golfo y de su entorno, acciones que España ha condenado sin excepción. Los ataques contra buques civiles y mercantes amenazan la estabilidad del conjunto de la región. Y la guerra ha reavivado los conflictos de Irak, el Líbano y Yemen.

    Por último, las guerras rara vez traen una paz duradera. Al contrario: ahondan los agravios y enquistan las divisiones que alimentan la violencia del mañana. La guerra de Rusia en Ucrania, por ejemplo, ha dinamitado la confianza en Moscú. El genocidio en Gaza ha exacerbado la indignación contra Israel, y eso podría desembocar en nuevas oleadas de terrorismo. Y la guerra contra Irán ha desestabilizado aún más la región y ha lastrado la cooperación entre sus países.

    In a recent development, el mundo tiene la responsabilidad de resistirse a la normalización de la guerra. Callar es un acto de cobardía y de complicidad. La sociedad española está dejando clara su posición: tres de cada cuatro españoles señalan la guerra como su mayor temor. Y un número aún mayor cree que se cierne otra guerra mundial.

    Recent findings suggest that pero no basta con condenar la guerra en abstracto. La ambición de acabar con ella debe ir acompañada de acciones concretas que hagan cada vez más difícil que los países inicien, sostengan y justifiquen un conflicto armado.

    Sources indicate that españa ha procurado actuar en esa dirección. Ha defendido las normas internacionales que marcan la diferencia entre un orden basado en reglas y otro gobernado por la fuerza. Y ha denunciado siempre los ataques armados que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas.

    Desde el primer día de la guerra en Gaza, España ha reclamado un alto el fuego inmediato y permanente, la liberación de todos los rehenes y la entrada sin restricciones de la ayuda humanitaria. En mayo de 2024, España reconoció el Estado de Palestina con la esperanza de que este paso contribuyera a avanzar hacia una solución negociada y duradera del conflicto. Y ha apoyado activamente los esfuerzos de la Corte Internacional de Justicia y de la Corte Penal Internacional para que los dirigentes israelíes rindan cuentas por sus violaciones del derecho internacional humanitario. Israel tenía derecho a la legítima defensa tras los atentados terroristas del 7 de octubre. Pero ese derecho no justifica el genocidio en Gaza ni la expansión de la ocupación ilegal de Cisjordania.

    In a recent development, disuadir la guerra exige también elevar el coste de la agresión. El resto del mundo debe asegurarse de que quien elija hacer la guerra no pueda hacerlo sin pagar un precio. A lo largo de la invasión rusa de Ucrania, por ejemplo, la Unión Europea ha aprobado sucesivas rondas de sanciones contra Rusia que España ha respaldado sin titubeos. España también ha prestado a Ucrania ayuda financiera, humanitaria y militar para que pueda defender su territorio y negarle a Rusia el botín de guerra.

    Los países deben negarse a ayudar a las partes a extender los conflictos en curso. España, por ejemplo, mantiene un embargo de armas a Israel desde 2023. Este año, además, negó a Estados Unidos el uso de su territorio y de sus instalaciones para la guerra contra Irán. La decisión de España no fue un acto de hostilidad hacia un aliado. Tampoco fue una expresión de neutralidad ni de simpatía hacia el régimen iraní. Fue el fruto de una valoración estratégica: implicarse habría favorecido la escalada del conflicto y agravado la inseguridad regional y mundial. Para ser fiel a su compromiso con la paz, España tenía que estar dispuesta a decir no, aunque eso tuviera un coste político. Si más países hubieran actuado igual, las guerras de Gaza y de Irán habrían sido mucho más difíciles y costosas de librar.

    According to recent reports, invertir en prosperidad es igualmente esencial. La seguridad crece cuando las sociedades son resilientes, las desigualdades se reducen y la ciudadanía puede confiar en las instituciones públicas. La decisión de España, el año pasado, de no asumir el objetivo de gasto en defensa del 5 % del PIB propuesto por la OTAN refleja esta visión. No nace de una falta de compromiso con la defensa europea. De hecho, mi Gobierno ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la autonomía estratégica de la Unión Europea, triplicando el gasto neto en defensa en los ocho años que llevo en el cargo. Pero la disuasión militar y el bienestar social deben reforzarse mutuamente. Al mantener un gasto en defensa proporcionado, España ha conservado el margen fiscal necesario para invertir 145.000 millones de euros adicionales en protección social, vivienda, sanidad y educación, y más de 30.000 millones en la transición ecológica. Son políticas que cohesionan la sociedad y, por tanto, la hacen más segura.

    Los esfuerzos de un solo país tienen, sin embargo, un alcance limitado. Cortarle el oxígeno a la guerra exige la implicación de todos: un esfuerzo colectivo basado en un multilateralismo genuino. Esta es la única estrategia que ha funcionado en el pasado. El sistema multilateral construido tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial abarcaba todo el planeta y contribuyó a preservar la paz entre las grandes potencias y a evitar una tercera guerra mundial.

    Reforzarlo no será tarea fácil. La pugna geopolítica y una desconfianza generalizada han debilitado a Naciones Unidas, los organismos financieros internacionales, las organizaciones regionales y otras instituciones multilaterales. Muchos países las perciben como ineficaces y atrapadas en una crisis perpetua, de modo que están recurriendo a marcos alternativos para intentar poner fin a las guerras.

    Algunos han optado por enfoques unilaterales, persiguiendo acuerdos transaccionales que acaban beneficiando a élites económicas y políticas y dejan al margen a las poblaciones afectadas por el conflicto. Los altos el fuego o los acuerdos de paz que logran pueden ser preferibles a la continuación de la guerra, pero cualquier paz impuesta por la ley del más fuerte, y no por el derecho, se asienta sobre cimientos frágiles.

    Otros países, frustrados con el multilateralismo, han intentado formar «coaliciones de voluntarios» u otros grupos «minilaterales» para garantizar su seguridad o alcanzar acuerdos ad hoc en materia de comercio o tecnología. Este enfoque puede ser una solución temporal a la parálisis de las instituciones tradicionales, pero su carácter excluyente fragmenta aún más un orden internacional ya dividido. Lo que necesitamos no es minilateralismo, sino maxilateralismo. La cooperación internacional alcanza su verdadera fuerza cuando es—o aspira a ser—universal. Dejar a una parte del mundo fuera de estos esfuerzos es, además, incubar la confrontación de mañana.

    According to recent reports, el sistema internacional del siglo XX no era perfecto. Sus normas se han aplicado de manera desigual, sus principios se han defendido de forma inconsistente y sus procedimientos han sido desesperantemente lentos. Pero es innegable que, sin él, el mundo sería un polvorín aún mayor. Basta un ejemplo: fue una red de tratados internacionales—entre ellos, el Tratado sobre la No Proliferación de las Armas Nucleares, el Tratado sobre Fuerzas Nucleares de Alcance Intermedio y el Tratado de Prohibición Parcial de los Ensayos Nucleares—la que puso fin a una carrera armamentística desbocada y extraordinariamente costosa que estaba llevando al mundo al borde de una guerra nuclear.

    Toda esta arquitectura institucional se está resquebrajando. Y sin ella, aspirar a preservar la paz es una quimera.

    Recent findings suggest that fortalecer las instituciones multilaterales debe ser el eje central de una campaña global para relegar la guerra a los libros de historia. Para ello será necesario acometer reformas de calado que les devuelvan la legitimidad y refuercen su capacidad de actuación, dando prioridad a las medidas que más contribuyan a la paz y la seguridad.

    La primera pasa por aumentar la representación en las Naciones Unidas y las instituciones de Bretton Woods. Actualizar la estructura del Consejo de Seguridad de Naciones Unidas es especialmente importante, dada su responsabilidad principal de mantener la paz internacional. Un Consejo de Seguridad con asientos permanentes y derecho de veto para las cinco potencias vencedoras de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, que en conjunto suman apenas una cuarta parte de la población mundial, no refleja el mundo de hoy. Debe ampliarse el número de miembros electos del Consejo y alargar su mandato más allá de los dos años actuales. Los nuevos asientos deben otorgarse principalmente a países de regiones infrarrepresentadas, en particular África y América Latina. Organizaciones regionales como la Unión Europea y la Unión Africana también deberían estar representadas en el Consejo, posiblemente ocupando puestos que hoy corresponden a Estados. Un Consejo de Seguridad más representativo no solo sería más justo, sino también más eficaz. Los países defienden y hacen cumplir con más empeño las normas internacionales cuando se sienten autores de ellas.

    According to recent reports, también hay que restringir estrictamente el poder de veto de los miembros permanentes, en especial cuando el Consejo de Seguridad delibere sobre casos de atrocidades masivas, genocidio, crímenes de lesa humanidad y crímenes de guerra. En última instancia, el veto debe abolirse por completo. Solo entonces podrá el Consejo responder a todos los actos de agresión sin quedar secuestrado por las objeciones de un solo Estado.

    Sources indicate that un espíritu similar debería orientar la transformación estructural de las instituciones financieras internacionales, en particular el Fondo Monetario Internacional y el Banco Mundial. La distribución del poder de voto en ambas sigue reflejando los equilibrios económicos del siglo XX y, por convención, un europeo está siempre al frente del FMI y un estadounidense, del Banco Mundial. Esto debe terminar. Las economías emergentes necesitan una representación más adecuada, y los puestos de liderazgo deben estar abiertos a todos los candidatos, sea cual sea su nacionalidad. También deberán evolucionar las responsabilidades que asumen en instituciones como la Organización Mundial del Comercio los países antes considerados «en desarrollo», a medida que crecen y se incorporan al grupo de las economías más ricas. Una gobernanza económica más justa aliviaría la desigualdad y el resentimiento que con tanta frecuencia atizan la inestabilidad y los conflictos.

    Otra reforma esencial consiste en revitalizar el marco internacional que contiene el riesgo de escalada nuclear. Parte de ese trabajo depende de las potencias nucleares. Corresponde a Estados Unidos y a Rusia negociar un tratado que suceda al acuerdo bilateral Nuevo START y que preserve topes verificables al despliegue de armas nucleares. Y, esta vez, China debería participar en las conversaciones.

    Pero el esfuerzo más amplio exige el compromiso de todos los países. Entre sus prioridades deben figurar la ratificación del Tratado de Prohibición Completa de los Ensayos Nucleares, para impedir que se reanuden las pruebas nucleares, y el avance de las negociaciones sobre un Tratado de Prohibición de la Producción de Material Fisionable, que prohibiría la producción de uranio altamente enriquecido y plutonio para armas nucleares. Todos deben también trabajar conjuntamente para regular el uso de la IA en el ámbito militar, especialmente en lo que respecta a las armas nucleares, a fin de preservar el control humano sobre las decisiones de lanzamiento y minimizar el riesgo de errores fatales. Los países no nucleares deben comprometerse a no adquirir armas nucleares y deben emplear todos los medios a su alcance para instar a las potencias nucleares a reducir sus arsenales, reforzar los mecanismos de verificación y reconstruir las salvaguardas diplomáticas que durante décadas han ayudado a evitar una catástrofe nuclear.

    Sources indicate that la tecnología puede contribuir en parte a esta tarea. Los avances en imágenes por satélite, sensores remotos y análisis de datos pueden aumentar la transparencia y la supervisión del cumplimiento de los acuerdos de control de armamentos. Pero también hay que hacer mucho más para evitar situaciones que puedan precipitar una guerra. Si los Estados con armas nucleares acuerdan reducir su disponibilidad operacional y reforzar la comunicación en momentos de tensión, los gobiernos contarán con más tiempo y más medios para desactivar las crisis. Cada país debe proteger sus sistemas de mando y control frente a los ciberataques y la manipulación informativa impulsada por la IA, de modo que una falsa alarma o un error de cálculo no desencadenen jamás una guerra nuclear.

    In a recent development, por último, es prioritario trabajar para garantizar que el sistema de justicia internacional pueda hacer cumplir las decisiones de los tribunales. Desmantelar la Corte Penal Internacional, como pretenden algunos países, solo aseguraría la impunidad de los crímenes más atroces. La CPI no solo debe investigar y juzgar los casos de genocidio, agresión, crímenes de guerra y crímenes de lesa humanidad, sino también contar con la autoridad necesaria para llevar ante la justicia a los responsables de esos crímenes. Cuando un Estado pasa a ser parte del Estatuto de Roma, el tratado que creó la CPI, acepta someterse a la jurisdicción de la Corte. Sin embargo, si ese Estado se niega a cooperar o a entregar a un sospechoso, no existe una sanción efectiva, sino apenas una llamada de atención. Esto debe cambiar. Los Estados que den cobijo a personas imputadas por la CPI deben afrontar consecuencias legales, diplomáticas y financieras. Iniciar y librar una guerra debe tener un coste real.

    Industry observers note that la reforma de las instituciones internacionales lleva años estancada, pero la próxima elección para la Secretaría General de Naciones Unidas ofrece una ocasión excepcional para darle un nuevo impulso. Que Naciones Unidas nombrara a su primera secretaria general sería un poderoso símbolo de renovación, inclusión y adaptación institucional. La organización no puede afirmar verdaderamente que habla en nombre de toda la humanidad mientras no la haya dirigido una mujer. Alcanzar este hito podría despertar una nueva ambición y reforzar la confianza en la capacidad de las instituciones internacionales para reformarse y para que recuperen su papel a la hora de poner freno a la guerra.

    According to recent reports, frenar la deriva del mundo hacia la guerra exigirá el compromiso más amplio posible. Ningún país, grande o pequeño, puede mirar hacia otro lado ni sumarse a las acciones que aviven la escalada. Todos debemos defender las normas internacionales que hoy ponen coto a la guerra y reformar y dotar de poder a las instituciones que mañana la harán imposible.

    Sources indicate that en última instancia, lo que hará inimaginable la guerra es una agenda de paz positiva que aborde las causas profundas de la inseguridad. Cada paso hacia la erradicación de la pobreza, la ampliación del acceso a una educación de calidad, el avance de la igualdad de género, el fortalecimiento de las instituciones democráticas y el aumento de la resiliencia ante los desastres naturales atenúa también las condiciones que engendran la violencia.

    Recent findings suggest that las instituciones financieras internacionales deben ser capaces de proporcionar financiación con rapidez, a gran escala y a un coste razonable, para que ningún país en desarrollo se vea obligado a elegir entre atender su deuda e invertir en su población. Los bancos multilaterales de desarrollo deben poder movilizar fondos para las transiciones ecológica y digital, de modo que las migraciones climáticas y la disputa por los recursos no se conviertan en detonantes de conflictos entre Estados. Y el Acuerdo sobre Pandemias de la Organización Mundial de la Salud debe ultimarse y entrar en vigor para garantizar que todos los países puedan acceder a vacunas y tratamientos cuando llegue la próxima emergencia sanitaria mundial.

    It has been revealed that por eso España ha procurado situar el desarrollo en el centro de su política exterior. El Gobierno español ha sido un firme defensor de los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible de la ONU para 2030 y, el año pasado, la ciudad de Sevilla acogió la Cuarta Conferencia Internacional sobre la Financiación para el Desarrollo, donde la comunidad internacional se comprometió a aligerar la carga de la deuda de los países vulnerables y a desbloquear inversiones para el desarrollo sostenible. España también ha promovido iniciativas como el Centro Global para Canjes de Deuda por Desarrollo, lanzado junto con el Banco Mundial; la Alianza multilateral por las Cláusulas de Suspensión de Deuda, que permite a los países vulnerables suspender el pago de su deuda tras una catástrofe; y un mecanismo propio para ofrecer hasta 60 millones de euros anuales en alivio de deuda a países en desarrollo. Además, España ha respaldado, junto con instituciones multilaterales y organizaciones internacionales, iniciativas de financiación climática, salud global, igualdad de género, seguridad alimentaria y protección social. Estas políticas de desarrollo son también políticas de construcción de paz.

    Un proyecto ambicioso de movilización global en favor del derecho internacional y de un multilateralismo genuino puede parecer poco realista. Pero ya hemos visto lo que ocurre cuando la normalización de la guerra arrastra a la humanidad al infierno. Los hombres y las mujeres que se levantaron de entre las ruinas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, el capítulo más oscuro de nuestra historia, encontraron la manera de construir un orden mundial multilateral. La pregunta a la que se enfrenta nuestra generación es si seremos capaces de preservar el imperio de la ley o permitiremos el regreso de la ley de la jungla. Si construiremos el mundo del mañana con visión de futuro y cooperación, o a través del caos y del dolor de otra guerra mundial. Debemos elegir bien mientras la decisión siga estando en nuestras manos.

    #145297. China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2780 w)

    China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.
    • NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
    • Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

    NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

    How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry.

    Lyle J. Goldstein and Nina Tannenwald.

    Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

    But the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

    There are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

    Recent findings suggest that china is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists announced that China was constructing 350 new nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-launched ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

    In a recent development, then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-debuted long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant fresh capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan concern stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

    As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

    Sources indicate that the Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is important to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

    China hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July New York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby mentioned, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-introduced cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

    It has been revealed that such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

    A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses new warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

    One of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

    In a recent development, beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

    Chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an important analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

    There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as important, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

    The United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

    The Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more vital, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

    Exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”.

    Another important step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

    Beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Senate just cleared the way for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, more commonly referred to as BAAJA.     Industry observers note that the U.S. Senate just cleared the way for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, more commonly referred to as BAAJA. The law aims to shorten review timelines for infrastructure projects and protect permits from later revocation, among other provisions. But beyond the technical details, the law has been notable for the unusual coalitions that have arranged in favor and opposed to it: Oil and gas companies, manufacturers, and labor unions are broadly in support, while environmental groups such as the Sierra Club and the Wilderness Society and progressive groups such as the NAACP have lined up against.

    What exactly would BAAJA do? Why has the law divided some trade unions against progressives? And can renewable energy outcompete fossil fuels on the free market?

    Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

    Cameron Abadi: What exactly would BAAJA do? And why is this just such a big issue right now in the United States?

    Adam Tooze: It’s basically an effort to streamline environmental review, restrict certain legal challenges, make permits—once they are issued—more secure. So, enabling investors to proceed robustly. And it’s aiming basically to enable a more rapid build-out of the electricity transmission system.

    It’s such a big deal because this is a really big problem. Electricity interconnection is a fiendishly difficult technical and legal issue. The Berkeley Lab found that about 2,600 gigawatts of generation and storage projects were seeking grid connection at the end of 2023. And more will have come online since. That’s about twice the existing capacity of the United States’ system. And they spend about five years at least applying for interconnection and entering commercial operation, compared to two years only as recently as a few decades ago. You’ve got projects like a giant wind project in Fresh Mexico, which is supposed to be a transmission line that connects New Mexico to Arizona. It took roughly 17 years from initial development to construction, and the vast majority of that was in the permitting. Pipelines are notorious for exactly the same reasons. So, Mountain Valley Pipeline, which is a gas pipeline 303 miles [long through West Virginia and Virginia], originally billed at $3.5 billion and now finally opened in 2024 at a cost of about $8 billion.

    Sources indicate that so there are a fundamental set of issues about not only how American procedures decide whether they are for or against significant infrastructure projects but also how long it takes them and how expensive they are. If we had a streamlined process, you could process a bunch of obstructions, do it rapidly, make a decision, move on. And instead, we have sort of the worst of both worlds, which is a lack of coherence, political chops, and changes by administrations, which are very pro-renewable energy, for instance, and then very opposed to it—which means that even when you do get the permits, they’re not secure. So it’s a mess.

    And this is a mess also against the backdrop of the last effort to break this impasse, which after all was the Biden administration. It’s certainly true now that AI is driving the conversation about the build-out of power supply in the United States. But the conversation started earlier with the push around Bidenomics, which then was instantiated in the form of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. And people like Brian Deese, who was a key architect of green industrial policy under the Biden administration, have mentioned that, you know, passing the Inflation Reduction Act without permitting reform produced modest results. Passing the Inflation Reduction Act with permitting reform would have made a huge difference. Passing the permitting reform two years before the Inflation Reduction Act had come into effect, setting the stage for the energy and the money that poured through the Inflation Reduction Act, would have been a complete game-changer. In other words, the pace of rollout would have been very dramatic. And I think that, in a sense, is what this conversation right now is about.

    And it’s furthermore crucial because it does expose fault lines within the coalitions that you might think of as being supportive to this. So Bidenomics glued a coalition together around the green energy project, around American reindustrialization, but also through extraordinarily complex coalition deals—the “everything bagel” liberalism, patching in a whole variety of different environmental justice groups, activists on behalf of rural America, activists on the behalf of minorities in the United States and underrepresented and discriminated-against communities—and they were all part of the Biden package. [Donald] Trump has blown that up. And what we’re seeing here is also a debate, I think, about what are the terms going to be under which a upcoming, energized Democratic majority actually attempts to restart the project of green modernization in the United States. That’s why this matters beyond the technicalities.

    In a recent development, CA: We tend to think of the left and unions as a natural coalition. But have there always been tensions between them that run along the fault lines of environmentalism, and is that what’s getting revealed in the debate around this law?

    Sources indicate that AT: In support of what I think is called BAAJA, you do see an unusually broad coalition of organized labor. It isn’t just building trade unions—sort of, you know, construction-happy pipeline workers or whatever. It is in fact a very broad coalition, including the AFL-CIO. And so, from their point of view, this is clearly an industrial, productivist kind of strategy. And it makes sense, and they’re not wrong. And the estimates are that this would move significant volumes of investment. Not stupendous, not dramatic. If you’ve actually seen the econometrics on this, the numbers are not overwhelming. But they’re real, and every little bit helps. And the obstruction around these issues has been highly significant in a number of individual cases. So the coalition is real.

    It has been revealed that but you’re right, there are also blocking oppositionists. In fact, it’s telling that in the Senate vote on the legislation so far the purple state senators—so senators who are exposed to more competitive races—were notably more supportive of this legislation than those in absolutely solid blue Democratic constituencies, where the leverage of other interests really came to the fore. And there are at least two that are very well worth taking seriously that have been articulated.

    Recent findings suggest that one is Bill McKibben, one of the real warhorses of the climate movement in the United States, who said, look, it’s all very well to say that we need an energy transition, so we need more electrical generation capacity and transmission facilities. This is clear. It is true. On the other hand, ultimately what counts here is the level of emissions. And so, more construction, more activity in this realm, is not an unalloyed and unambiguous benefit. And if it’s possible that these changes might in fact open the door to large-scale fossil build-out, then, in fact, this is really an ambiguous a set of proposals. And it’s quite clear that in its bipartisan nature, a little bit like some of the Biden administration legislation as well, they are trying to provide pork and trying to buy support from energy interests across the board.

    Industry observers note that and then the other constituency that you might think of as left is represented by a spokesperson like Abigail Dillen of Earthjustice, who is representing what in the American conversation is called an environmental justice point of view, first and foremost. And so, just for clarification’s sake, environmental politics is a very broad church. Climate politics within that comes in different shades as well, but climate politics has this very macroscopic, ultimately global point of view. And one of the answers given by the establishment with regards to climate politics is simply electrify everything, build as much clean energy infrastructure as possible as quickly as possible. But the consequences of that locally can of course be very, very disruptive, not to say incredibly damaging. And this is where the environmental justice movement comes in in the United States, which has a genealogy which really originates in the 1980s and 1990s, centrally concerned with the interests of marginalized communities in the United States, notably Black communities in the American South, who find themselves systematically in harm’s way when it comes to otherwise perhaps interesting and notable industrial expansion. And so her argument, and the opposition of environmental justice campaigners around this, is to say, well, it’s all very well that you open the door to this kind of development, but who walks through that door? Which interests are going to take advantage of this, and who is going to lose out?

    Recent findings suggest that and to go back to your substantial-picture historical question, what you’re seeing there is a confrontation between, if you like, three generations of American radical and progressive politics. One is the classic New Deal productivist coalition, which is about a bigger government and facilitating public-private partnerships in various ways that enable large-scale investment and development. And that had very considerable buy-in from trade unions.

    Expanding the U.S. grid is vital to staying globally competitive.

    But what we see from the 1960s onward—not necessarily in hostility to organized labor but recognizing the impact of the success of this kind of development and its lopsidedness and its egalitarian tendencies—are the other two constituencies of American progressivism, which are now speaking their voice. These things didn’t emerge at the same time in the 1930s, but you could say in the 1960s we see the development of the ecological movement in the United States, the broad-based opposition to environmental damage, which in many cases has a distinctly upper-middle-class, Sierra Club kind of feel to it.

    And then from the late 1970s, 1980s, onward, the environmental justice movement, which is in a sense environmental politics crossed with the Civil Rights Movement in the United States and focusing on environmental problems. And those three things together come out of the same tradition of American progressivism, you might say, but they are not necessarily on the same page. And their targets are not necessarily the same thing either. And the work that Bidenomics did was to, in some senses, square that circle. And as we’ve said, that’s the coalition that needs to be rebuilt. And this is a conversation about how that gets done.

    In a recent development, CA: One often hears that renewables now outcompete other sources of energy on economic terms. So why shouldn’t advocates for renewables prefer a law that would presumably create a freer market?

    AT: Well, those kind of claims are based on what are so-called comparisons of unsubsidized levelized costs of fresh electricity generation. That’s the standard measure. And outfits like Lazard have produced numbers that show, for instance, that onshore wind can be had for a cost of between $37 and $99 per megawatt hour, utility-scale solar for between $40 and $98, combined-cycle natural gas for $51 to $129, and so on and so forth.

    And when you make the comparisons on that basis, it’s generally true that solar and onshore wind come out as the optimum strategies. But they’re very, very partial measures of cost. Because what they don’t really account for is intermittency fundamentally. Right now, we really shouldn’t be making comparisons of just pure solar and wind versus gas because gas can be turned on and off once you’ve got the infrastructure. Whereas obviously solar and rain can’t. It depends on the availability of sunshine and wind. So they need to be backed up by batteries. Once you do the backup by batteries, they’re still competitive, but the argument is not as simple as saying that they’re the cheapest.

    But broadly speaking, I, in fact, entirely agree with the general thrust of your message. I’m an optimist on this question. And I think this is also the position, for instance, of the abundance agenda types, [Ezra] Klein and [Derek] Thompson and so on, which is that it’s a totally reasonable argument to make—namely that in the end, these technologies are superior. They are cheaper. People are investing in them. If you look in the pipeline, the pipeline is overwhelmingly renewables. And that’s not for reasons of wokeness. There are issues of intermittency, but the harder we push at this, the more we invest, the more the urgency will be to find solutions to them. And markets that are relatively free, like that of Texas, for instance, have turned out to be huge pioneers of rapid adoption of solar and wind. So I think, broadly speaking, that argument is well merited.

    Industry observers note that the risk is—and this is where somebody like a McKibben will come in—would be to say, well, that’s all very well, but at the margin, we can’t be certain that this game will play out necessarily in the favor of renewables. And the argument here is not coal anymore. Once upon a time, you might have said coal could come back as a source of electricity generation. I think that argument is done everywhere outside China, probably. [There are] very few places in the world where coal makes any sense. Nuclear, for those who have environmental concerns about nuclear, [is] also prohibitively expensive. A free market option without subsidy probably kills it completely stone-dead given its costs. The real matter is gas.

    It has been revealed that and the lesson here is not abstract—it’s historical. Because in the 2010s, what happened is that the entire calculus of the electricity-generating investment game in the United States was changed by the sudden availability of huge quantities of dirt-cheap shale gas, so fracked gas. And that had the effect of considerably displacing the adoption of wind and solar, which actually progressed more rapidly in Europe because gas prices—despite all of the talk of cheap gas from Russia, it was always nonsense. The really cheap gas comes from Texas, it comes from Pennsylvania, it comes from shale in the United States. And that considerably slowed down the adoption of more sustainable, more renewable energy sources. But broadly speaking, of course, it’s still a win. And folks from within the Obama administration embraced this under the heading of “all of the above” because gas replacing coal is a net win in terms of emissions. You might quibble with this if you think about the methane admitted in the production of gas, but nevertheless, it is a step in the right direction.

    In a recent development, so the general thrust of your question, I think, should be affirmed. You know, we should not be thinking of renewables as a sort of endangered technology that needs protecting against the substantial beasts of fossil industry. Are there fossil risks? Yes, but they come largely from innovation in the fossil sector and not the old enemies. Not coal, not nuclear—oil has never really been in the game here anyway for electricity generation, not since the ’70s. But that, to my mind, means that this should be weighed up in terms of exactly how much build-out of which types of energy we expect. It’s not a matter of principle that renewables should favor regulation, fossils should favor deregulation. It’s not as simple as that. It’s a conjunctural specific historical gamble that, in the current moment, the benefits outweigh the downsides.

    Recent findings suggest that what we’re seeing, unfortunately, under Trump is that the biggest build-out and the biggest acceleration of electricity demand in American history—in recent times at least—probably ever in American history actually in terms of sheer volume, is taking place under an administration that seems determined to block renewables and under a permitting system that doesn’t permit a rapid build-out of efficient capacity. And the disaster there is it’s channeling all of that AI demand into gas-fired generation. It’s not epic by global standards; this isn’t China’s coal build-out. But it’s taking America in the wrong direction. And that’s the backdrop also against which this conversation is taking place right now. We see that there is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity or historic opportunity to have accelerated American electrification along green lines, and it’s being obstructed.

    Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi.

    In a recent development, adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze.
