    #145292. Why Israel Is Losing America

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2401 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Israel Is Losing America

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress.
    • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Key Ally.
    • Sources indicate that american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Problems on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

    Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Key Ally.

    Sources indicate that american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

    Sources indicate that as I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

    Recent findings suggest that things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a fresh paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

    According to recent reports, this change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

    Whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a upcoming U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

    Trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

    Time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace strategy for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is at the moment marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

    Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he stated himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

    It has been revealed that trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

    Recent findings suggest that trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

    Unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising fresh ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

    Recent findings suggest that israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, revealed wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

    In a recent development, israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

    Without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

    Recent findings suggest that it is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

    Recent findings suggest that israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s blueprint for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

    Israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

    In a recent development, israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of latest Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

    In a recent development, israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

    It has been revealed that these steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

    Industry observers note that if Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

    #145291. Latest Update: Democrats unveil 2028 debate rules with new dark money restrictions for presidential hopefuls

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (714 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foxnews ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Democrats unveil 2028 debate rules with new dark money restrictions for presidential hopefuls

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Democratic strategist John McCarthy discusses the DNC’s upcoming mandatory pledge for 2028 candidates to swear off of dark money in the primary.
    • The 2028 election season is already off to the races.
    • The Democratic Party released its rules of engagement for the next presidential primary season on Monday morning, outlining a framework for 12 debates and setting barriers for candidates hoping to compete.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democratic strategist John McCarthy discusses the DNC’s upcoming mandatory pledge for 2028 candidates to swear off of dark money in the primary.

    The 2028 election season is already off to the races.

    The Democratic Party released its rules of engagement for the next presidential primary season on Monday morning, outlining a framework for 12 debates and setting barriers for candidates hoping to compete.

    One key rule will have Democratic presidential hopefuls swear off dark money during the course of the primary election.

    "In the wake of the Citizens United Supreme Court decision, dark money and independent spending have exploded, increasing the influence of special interests in politics," a press release by the Democratic National Committee (DNC) mentioned. "While the DNC does not have the legal authority to ban super PACs or dark money groups, we are requiring our candidates to denounce their involvement in the Democratic presidential primary, in line with Democratic Party values and our 2024 Platform, in order to qualify for the debate stage.".

    HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS.

    Democratic presidential candidates arrive on stage for the Democratic presidential primary debate at the Charleston Gaillard Center on Feb. 25, 2020, in Charleston, S.C. (Scott Olson/Getty Images).

    That includes money earned by both super PACs and 501(c)(4) nonprofit organizations during the course of the entire primary.

    And the rule, according to a framework obtained by Fox News Digital, will rely largely on Democrats' own self-reporting.

    Each campaign must designate a go-between with the DNC whose job is to specifically identify and report spending by outside dark money groups.

    DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT MAKES DAMNING ADMISSION AS GOP PROBES FOREIGN DONATION ALLEGATIONS.

    If outside groups spend money on a specific candidate that remarked candidate did not approve, they must denounce the action to still qualify for primary debates.

    Democratic presidential candidates debate each other on NBC News in June 2019 in Miami. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images).

    If the candidate does approve or request the spending, they are required to refund those dollars and provide proof of doing so.

    Industry observers note that "This is a framework, and it's the first step. There's going to be more granularity that comes over the next few months as the field takes shape. So this is kind of the opening of a conversation," Democratic strategist John McCarthy told Fox News Digital on Monday. "I think it's good that we're having this opening of a conversation because it will put pressure on all of the candidates internally to sit and say, we're going to lock arms and embody our values as Democrats.".

    Asked about whether the emphasis on self-reporting will be a strong enough guardrail given the lack of laws around dark money spending, McCarthy suggested pressure from the party base will help.

    "I think if someone doesn't wanna make that pledge, I don't think that they're going to be rewarded by our primary voters as someone who they want to move forward as our nominee," McCarthy noted.

    And while the pledge explicitly talks about the primary, it leaves open the question of dark money spending in the general election.

    It has been revealed that DNC Chair Ken Martin makes a speech during the press conference for the DNC site visit at Ball Arena in Denver on May 6, 2026. (Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post via Getty Images).

    But McCarthy suggested that it would not hurt whoever the Democrats' eventual nominee will be.

    "I think that Democrat-on-Democrat fighting is not going to enhance us for the general election," he remarked.

    #145290. After ‘Wild Horse Nine,’ 5 of the Best Movies About the CIA

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2177 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    After ‘Wild Horse Nine,’ 5 of the Best Movies About the CIA

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In Martin McDonagh’s upcoming film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.
    • “You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character.
    • In Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    In Martin McDonagh’s upcoming film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.

    “You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character. “There’s whole countries that wouldn’t be free if not for you. Guatemala. Indonesia. That place in Africa I can never remember the name of. Sure you killed some people. So fucking what?” Do people who work at the CIA really talk this way? God, I hope not.

    In Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.

    “You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character. “There’s whole countries that wouldn’t be free if not for you. Guatemala. Indonesia. That place in Africa I can never remember the name of. Sure you killed some people. So fucking what?” Do people who work at the CIA really talk this way? God, I hope not.

    In a recent development, but then again, Wild Horse Nine, set during the 1973 Chilean coup, isn’t really about the CIA. The dark comedy—a good bet for landing several Academy Award nominations—is about mortality and remorse and how even the most brazen people can have moments of clarity and reevaluate their past actions. It uses the CIA as a skin, the way McDonagh’s previous (and very similar) fatalistic comedy In Bruges did with contract killers.

    It has been revealed that although its average employee likely has a job as mundane as any other government worker, an organization as key to world affairs and as necessarily shrouded in mystery as the CIA is understandably a great font for storytellers. But I can’t say there have been too many classic films that treat the CIA seriously.

    There have been some marvelous paranoid thrillers, specifically Watergate-era classics like Three Days of the Condor, which tend to get a little far-fetched by the third act. There are some exceptions, like 2005’s Syriana and 2014’s A Most Wanted Man, that show the minutiae of spy craft in a compelling way that doesn’t devolve into silliness. These are rarities. I also don’t really consider Sicario or Zero Dark Thirty CIA films, because their sweep covers multiple government agencies.

    The lengthy 2006 film The Good Shepherd, directed by Robert De Niro and starring Matt Damon, was an attempt to show how the agency grew out of Yale secret societies and reached a crisis point during the Bay of Pigs. Despite some good intentions, though, the movie is a significant dud and has few champions. (I recently revisited the film, but found myself needing several attempts, after I fell asleep on the couch on more than one occasion.).

    Even for pure action-adventure absurdity, Britain has James Bond, but the United States has … James Bond’s friend Felix Leiter? Nice guy and all, but not 007. Mission: Impossible’s Ethan Hunt works for the Impossible Missions Force, remember, not the CIA. In the 1960s, Derek Flint, a Bond knockoff, worked for Z.O.W.I.E. (Zonal Organization World Intelligence Espionage), and Matt Helm worked for ICE (Intelligence and Counter-Espionage). Other than Jack Ryan, whose recent Amazon series and films have been absolutely horrible, Hollywood hasn’t given us a CIA man who’s become a household name.

    There have, of course, been great movies about the CIA, but all of them are laced with comedy. Maybe this is some kind of national defense mechanism? Hey, don’t mind us, we may be tinkering in the affairs of other sovereign nations, but we know it’s a little naughty.

    If the dark comedy of Wild Horse Nine has you itching for more examples of this curious phenomenon, here are five titles you can stream—all of which are intellectually zesty and a great deal of fun. (The Good Shepherd has value, too, should you find your stash of zolpidem depleted.) I’ve listed them from least-to-most zany.

    Bryan Cranston and Ben Affleck in Argo.IMDB.

    This extremely watchable spy movie—with a healthy dose of comedy—was a major financial success and also won the Academy Award for best picture. (It beat both Steven Spielberg’s Lincoln and the aforementioned Zero Dark Thirty, both of which I’d place higher, but much like an operation to destabilize a country’s democracy, Oscar success isn’t always predictable.).

    The story is rooted in a true event: During the Iran hostage crisis, a CIA agent (Affleck) created an elaborate cover story to smuggle home six Americans who were hiding with the Canadian ambassador. His cockamamie plan was to fake being a Canadian film production that was scouting for locations. To make it work, there had to be a real script (a Star Wars knockoff) plus actual Hollywood producers and craftspeople—so Alan Arkin and John Goodman (playing John Chambers, the real-life guy who did the prosthetics for Planet of the Apes) join in.

    It has been revealed that naturally, there are setbacks and raised stakes as the baddies piece together which Americans are missing, then there’s a race against the clock for the massive finish. Sadly (well, not for the real people involved), the action-adventure elements of the last act were made up for the movie. But Argo is still an engrossing heist-style picture. It has respect for the CIA, but also presents an agency with a prankster’s edge.

    Funnily enough, a 1966 crime-comedy from Italian director Vittorio De Sica and Fresh York playwright Neil Simon called After the Fox used the idea of a fake movie production as the cover for a grand scheme—but in their case, it was smuggling gold.

    In a recent development, more recently, a group of Hollywood producers used the Argo technique as cover for an actual scheme in Poland, trying to recover a cache of stamps believed stolen from concentration camp prisoners. They even made a documentary film, The Stamp Thief, about the charade.

    It has been revealed that julia Roberts and Tom Hanks in Charlie Wilson’s War. IMDB.

    In a recent development, in the months after 9/11, like many freaked-out Americans, I would stay up until dawn watching cable news stations, which is where I first learned the term “blowback,” and about how some felt that the CIA’s backing of the Mujahideen against the Soviets in Afghanistan caused a domino effect that eventually knocked down the Twin Towers. If I tried to explain what I’d seen the night before on C-SPAN 2, I sounded a bit like a paranoid lunatic, so I was very happy when screenwriter Aaron Sorkin and director Mike Nichols collaborated on Charlie Wilson’s War, a scathingly dark CIA satire that summed a lot of this up.

    The always affable Tom Hanks stars as the sleazy titular congressman who, from a Vegas hot tub filled with Playboy models, sees a 60 Minutes report about Afghan refugees. It’s 1980, and he’s worried about Soviet encroachment, but also finds himself (somewhat to his surprise) genuinely caring about civilians caught up in large geopolitical events.

    According to recent reports, he finds likeminded spirits in Joanne Herring (Julia Roberts), a wealthy Houston socialite and political activist, and Gust Avrakotos (Philip Seymour Hoffman), a working-class CIA operative with a brilliant mind, well-honed bullshit detector, and extremely short temper who was just passed over for promotion. Like Argo, Charlie Wilson’s War is practically a heist picture, but about pushing levers in Washington to quietly appropriate funds and bring matériel to the Afghan fighters.

    Industry observers note that the dark punchline, of course, is how our heroes are powerless when it comes time to “win the peace,” as it were, leaving a power vacuum that, it can easily be argued, was filled by al Qaeda. The film’s release at the end of George W. Bush’s presidency functioned as a needed release valve.

    Walter Matthau in Hopscotch.IMDB.

    Industry observers note that quite the opposite of seductive Sean-Connery-as-007 is hangdog Walter Matthau, but the dark comedy Hopscotch suggests they have some traits in common. Matthau plays Miles Kendig, a veteran CIA agent whose boss (Ned Beatty) takes him out of the field and sticks him with a desk job. As revenge, Kendig decides he’ll write his memoirs (much like Malkovich in Wild Horse Nine), and his spilled secrets make security agencies across the globe very nervous. As he sends salacious excerpts to international higher-ups from various international hiding spots, one of the few things the CIA and KGB can agree upon is: Get Matthau away from his typewriter!

    Aiding him is an old flame (Glenda Jackson, who also starred with Matthau’s in the popular comedy House Calls) who lives in Austria, which is a nice touch because our lead character is an opera nut who likes to sing along (poorly) to Mozart in the car.

    Industry observers note that what Hopscotch has in common with Charlie Wilson’s War is presenting CIA bosses as absolute buffoons. The best part is when Matthau uses Beatty’s own vacation home as a hideout—which America’s intelligence forces then shoot to pieces. While Walter Matthau circa 1980 isn’t the most athletic secret agent, he’s quick with disguises, voices, thinking on his feet, and laying out elaborate traps. This is a great old school comedy with just enough post-Watergate negativity to keep it sharp.

    Alan Arkin and Peter Falk in The In-Laws.IMDB.

    Hopscotch is a little wacky. The In-Laws is full-on madcap. It’s also one of the funniest movies ever made, though its serpentine plot is hard to explain in just a few sentences. But I’ll give it a go….

    It has been revealed that alan Arkin plays a nervous dentist whose daughter is getting married to a nice kid, but Arkin hasn’t yet met the boy’s family. Turns out the father, played by Peter Falk, is a noisy madman who is either bank robber or a rogue CIA agent with blockhead bosses in the middle of an elaborate scheme to overthrow a Latin American dictator. Things soon spiral out of control, and this odd couple find themselves in several high-speed chases, dodging bullets while still hoping to make it to the wedding in time. The two great actors zing each other with quality barbs, and when that’s been exhausted there’s some physical comedy, too.

    The screenplay, written by Andrew Bergman, who also worked on Blazing Saddles, Fletch, and Soapdish, offers a much milder version of the impudence toward the CIA that you see in Wild Horse Nine. “You win some, you lose some,” Peter Falk shrugs when asked about the Bay of Pigs. Though this movie is mostly a comedic joy, the notion that U.S. intelligence is in the hands of nutcases at best—or sheer incompetents at worst—finds quick purchase here and seems to have reverberated in the decades since.

    Brad Pitt and Frances McDormand in Burn After Reading. IMDB.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s a lot about John Malkovich’s Wild Horse Nine character, Chris Carlisle, that may feel familiar. In Burn After Reading, the Coen brothers’ shaggiest movie (besides The Major Lebowski), Malkovich plays Osborne Cox, a CIA agent who is demoted and decides to write a vicious memoir. But unlike the overlooked and pen-poised agents mentioned on this list already, Cox is a complete klutz.

    But so is everyone in this tale, which includes Brad Pitt as dunderhead gym trainer Chad Feldheimer who, after a wild string of goof-ups and misunderstandings, ends up with a computer disc holding the first draft of Cox’s book. Feldheimer thinks he’s stumbled upon some serious material (it’s really just drunken grievances) and decides to blackmail Cox. This does not go well, and a ripple effect includes a murderer’s row of daffy performances from George Clooney, Frances McDormand, Richard Jenkins (more dumb than daffy), J.K. Simmons (exasperated by the stupidity around him, but powerless), and others.

    This was the Coen brothers’ follow-up to No Country For Old Men, their Oscar-winning crime drama based on Cormac McCarthy’s dark tale of greed and fate, and it’s probably the most cartoonish thing they’ve ever done. The CIA is nothing but a punching bag for 96 minutes, but the remaining undercurrent of violence erupts from time to time in some shocking (but hilarious) moments. Burn After Reading pushes the silliness to the absolute edge, but still somehow feels like parts of it could be true.

    Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central New Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman.

    SolarEdge unveils U.S.-made optimizer for C&I solar

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • SolarEdge’s latest Duo Power Optimizer promises to simplify commercial and industrial solar installations with 50% fewer optimizer units, independent module-level power tracking, and enhanced safety features.
    • According to recent reports, the commercial and industrial (C&I) solar market is getting a fresh hardware option aimed at making installations simpler without sacrificing system performance.
    • Industry observers note that announced November 16 ahead of RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, the upcoming product introduces a 2:1 architecture that allows one optimizer to connect two solar modules.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    SolarEdge’s latest Duo Power Optimizer promises to simplify commercial and industrial solar installations with 50% fewer optimizer units, independent module-level power tracking, and enhanced safety features.

    According to recent reports, the commercial and industrial (C&I) solar market is getting a fresh hardware option aimed at making installations simpler without sacrificing system performance. SolarEdge Technologies has unveiled its new Duo Power Optimizer, a U.S.-manufactured solution designed to deliver module-level energy harvesting and monitoring while cutting the number of power optimizers in half.

    Industry observers note that announced November 16 ahead of RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, the upcoming product introduces a 2:1 architecture that allows one optimizer to connect two solar modules. Notably, each module retains its own independent maximum power point tracker (MPPT), which preserves the module-level performance benefits associated with the traditional one-to-one optimizer configurations.

    For developers, EPCs and installers managing large-scale rooftop and distributed generation projects, the value here lies in fewer components to purchase, wire and install, with no trade-off in module-level optimization.

    Simplifying installation without sacrificing performance.

    SolarEdge’s optimization tech addresses the challenge of conventional string inverter systems, which is that an underperforming module can affect the output of an entire string. But by allowing each module to operate independently, the system limits the impact of shading, degradation or performance differences between panels.

    According to recent reports, the Duo brings demonstrates that capability in a two-module configuration. By reducing the number of optimizers by 50% compared with one-to-one designs, SolarEdge is targeting an opportunity to streamline balance-of-system requirements and reduce the installation labor.

    It has been revealed that solarEdge’s U.S.-made Duo Power Optimizer connects two solar modules while maintaining independent module-level power tracking for commercial and industrial solar installations. Credit: SolarEdge.

    The hardware also incorporates design changes intended to improve jobsite efficiency. Each optimizer features two input pairs: a shorter connection for the nearest module and a pre-extended connection for the adjacent module. The arrangement reduces excess wiring and eliminates the need for field-made jumpers.

    The configuration also accommodates modules with different orientations, making it particularly relevant for east-west and dual-tilt racking applications.

    Safety moves closer to the module.

    Beyond installation efficiency, SolarEdge is emphasizing electrical safety as a central feature of the upcoming product.

    The Duo extends the company’s Sense Connect technology to its input and output connectors, monitoring connector temperatures to identify developing challenges before they potentially escalate into overheating or electrical arcs.

    Recent findings suggest that also, the optimizer introduces what SolarEdge describes as an industry-first approach to arc fault detection: every optimizer acts as an individual arc sensor. Rather than relying exclusively on detection at the inverter, the system distributes monitoring throughout the array, allowing potential arc faults to be identified closer to their source.

    Recent findings suggest that solarEdge says the technology provides coverage across strings with up to 3,280 feet of total cable length between the inverter and optimizer. It can also help pinpoint problems to the optimizer area, potentially making troubleshooting and maintenance more efficient.

    Industry observers note that manufactured at SolarEdge’s Florida facility, the Duo is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements, according to the firm. SolarEdge claims its domestic-content eligibility levels are consistent with those of its previous U.S.-manufactured power optimizers, subject to applicable tax guidance and project-specific requirements.

    A practical play for the C&I market.

    For SolarEdge, the Duo represents an effort to combine three priorities that are becoming more and more important in commercial solar: installation efficiency, system-level safety, and domestic manufacturing.

    In a recent development, the technology does not fundamentally change the value proposition of module-level optimization. Instead, it looks to make that architecture more economical and easier to deploy at scale.

    SolarEdge will showcase the Duo Power Optimizer at RE+ 2026.

    #145287. Tech Report: The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2261 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.
    • It has been revealed that since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested.
    • According to recent reports, turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.

    Ankara’s Risky Bid to Impose Regional Order.

    It has been revealed that since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested. The previous Gulf-centered order had Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) trying to stabilize and shape the region using economic statecraft and the normalization of relations with former foes in Iran, Israel, Turkey, and Syria. Three years of war in Gaza, and more recently in Iran and the Gulf, have severely disrupted that order-building project and generated a deep sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

    According to recent reports, turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum. Before 2023, Ankara’s influence had been in decline; after years of diplomatic isolation following the Arab uprisings, it had just begun repairing its ties with major regional actors. But in the past few years, Turkey has earned American backing for its policies in Syria and its regional diplomacy, and it has made an effort to secure the home front by pursuing a peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a militant group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state. Most recently, in August, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey signed the Mecca Defense Alliance, a collective security agreement that institutionalizes Turkey’s regional positioning and pulls the country directly into Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis.

    It has been revealed that turkey’s post–October 7 strategy has restored the country’s position as a regional heavyweight. But it is not capable of meeting its larger objective: establishing order on its own terms. Turkey, like the region’s other aspiring leaders, lacks the power to impose a new security framework on its own. Its nascent efforts to build one, such as the new Mecca pact, merely make countries outside the bloc feel unsafe, feeding instability. Turkey’s most ambitious plays for regional leadership are therefore likely to prove ineffective or even counterproductive. As long as the Middle East’s highly militarized, zero-sum security dynamics remain, Ankara would be better off concentrating on interests closer to home that it has the power to protect.

    Industry observers note that this is not the first time that Turkey has tried to shape the broader Middle Eastern order. Ankara saw the Arab uprisings in the early 2010s as a historic window of opportunity. The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) described the political transformation sweeping the region as “the people’s coming to power,” and the Turkish government expected that eventual elections in the Arab countries rocked by protest would bring into office parties aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood, which was ideologically sympathetic and had practical links to the AKP. The emergence of friendly governments, the thinking went, would increase Turkey’s influence in the region.

    Yet these hopes soon receded. Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood–affiliated president, Mohamed Morsi, was overthrown in 2013, and Turkey’s bet on the opposition movement in Syria failed as Bashar al-Assad clung to power. Turkey was left isolated. A rival axis composed of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE objected to Turkey’s Muslim Brotherhood ties and sought to limit Ankara’s influence. This group contested Turkey’s positions across the Middle East, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Horn of Africa, effectively fighting proxy battles with Turkey in conflicts in Libya, Somalia, and Syria.

    Then, the attacks on October 7, 2023, ushered in another period of upheaval. Some changes since have played in Turkey’s favor. Chief among them is the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024 at the hands of opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Turkey had arguably invested more than any other country in pursuit of regime change in Damascus; it assisted opposition groups for years. Yet as the years went by, that objective seemed increasingly out of reach. The region’s other major powers made their peace with the regime’s survival, and even Ankara began considering rapprochement with Assad to avoid being left out in the cold. Assad’s fall changed Turkey’s fortunes overnight, handing it a level of influence in Syria it had not held in more than a decade.

    Other developments proved more dangerous for Ankara. Israel’s foreign policy became more assertive and revisionist after October 7, and its expansive security objectives began to clash with Turkey’s own. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s sharp criticism of Israeli policies in Gaza strained the relationship, and it deteriorated further when Turkey expanded its foothold in post-Assad Syria and Israel came to view Ankara’s military presence there as a direct threat. As Israel continues to strike sites in Syria—attacks Ankara has condemned—the risk of escalation is only growing. A miscalculation on either side could lead to a direct clash between Israeli and Turkish forces.

    The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, meanwhile, has cut both ways for Turkey. While Tehran’s attention has been focused elsewhere, Ankara has welcomed Iran’s retreat from Syria and the chance to push back against its remaining influence in Iraq. Turkey also has no interest in seeing a nuclear-armed Iran upend the regional balance of power. Yet the prospect of chaos across Turkey’s eastern border, should the Iranian regime fall, has bred real anxiety in Ankara, as has the possibility that Iran could become emboldened if the regime emerges from the war intact.

    In this complex environment, Ankara has pursued a three-pronged strategy to protect its security interests and, it hopes, capitalize on opportunities the upheaval has created. Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to power, Erdogan has drawn Turkey closer to the United States and tried to use his relationship with Washington to advance Ankara’s regional policies. Turkey has also pressed ahead with regional normalization, building on efforts to repair ties with Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other key Arab countries in the early 2020s, with the aim to forge a broader regional bloc. And, domestically, Ankara rolled out the “Turkey Without Terror” process, an attempt to resolve the conflict with the PKK inside and outside Turkey, which Turkey’s adversaries have long exploited by arming Kurdish groups or backing them politically.

    Some of Ankara’s policies have borne fruit. Consider, for instance, the outreach to Washington. Erdogan’s close relations with Trump helped bring the United States on board with Turkey’s expanded role in Syria. Turkey was one of the four countries Washington brought in to help negotiate the U.S.-proposed October 2025 cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas, and as a result, Trump offered and Erdogan accepted a seat on the U.S. president’s so-called Board of Peace for Gaza’s reconstruction. Turkey has played an active part mediating between the United States and Iran during the latest war. And Trump publicly endorsed the Mecca Defense Alliance, calling it “massive, bold, and key.” All of this points to a recognition in Washington of Turkey’s regional importance, the U.S. administration’s willingness to support some of Ankara’s priorities, and Turkey’s determination to elevate its own position.

    Sources indicate that yet there are undeniable limits to Turkey’s quest for influence. At a February 2026 Board of Peace summit, for instance, Turkey was excluded from participating in a planned international troop deployment and police training in Gaza—a sign that warming relations with Washington were not enough to override Israeli objections to having a Turkish military footprint in the Palestinian territory. In Syria, similarly, the support Turkey has secured from the Trump administration has not stopped Israel from launching military strikes at Syrian targets near Turkish positions. Simply put, Turkey has not been able to use its relationship with the Trump administration to overcome the limit Israeli opposition places on the scope of Turkey’s regional role.

    Turkey’s regional normalization efforts have yielded mixed results, too. Restoring diplomatic ties with significant players such as Saudi Arabia is in Turkey’s interest, to be sure. But the alliances Ankara is entering with these countries risk making Turkey and the region less secure, not more. The Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could end up hardening rival blocs and elevating regional tensions. Turkey insists that the alliance is directed against no country in particular and has suggested that Egypt, Syria, or even Iran could eventually join. But in the meantime, Iran, Israel, and the Houthis could see it as a threat and try to test or weaken its members’ commitment.

    Furthermore, the pact could pull Turkey into other countries’ wars. That possibility is already on the table now that the Turkish parliament has ratified the agreement and the Houthis are escalating their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government has insisted that any military support it provided would be confined to deterrence, intelligence sharing, and defense-industrial cooperation. Yet Saudi Arabia is now seeking Pakistan’s and Turkey’s help with air defense and territorial protection, and the three states have agreed to prepare forces for rapid deployment. Sending Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia would still require separate parliamentary approval. If parliament allowed it, even a limited deployment would risk drawing Turkey into a wider regional conflict.

    Some kind of regional security framework is necessary. The problem is that no country in the region, including Turkey, has the power to impose a security order on the rest, so whenever someone tries, other countries feel threatened. An informal cooperation framework that is open to all countries in the region—and that asks its members to commit to nonaggression instead of making mutual-defense pledges—might work better. But the assembly and functioning of such a coalition require trust that governments in the region do not have. Breaking the impasse would likely require the United States to play a more constructive role than it has in recent years—not simply endorsing whatever regional arrangement emerges, as Trump did with the Mecca pact, or pressuring countries to normalize relations with Israel without expecting Israel to change its policies in return, as Trump has also done. Instead, Washington, perhaps with the help of Beijing, would need to compel regional rivals such as Iran and Saudi Arabia to take confidence-building measures that would make an inclusive security framework viable in the long run. Without this external push, the narrower security blocs that emerge in the region will only lead to further instability.

    Ankara’s strongest cards lie closer to home. The Kurdish peace process has moved slowly since February 2025, when Abdullah Ocalan, the imprisoned leader of the PKK, called on the militant group to disarm. But it has yielded tangible progress. In May 2025, the PKK declared that it would dissolve. In Syria, Kurdish forces are being integrated into the Syrian army, and Mazloum Abdi, the commander of the People’s Defense Units, a Kurdish armed group affiliated with the PKK, was appointed as a presidential adviser in August. Syria’s postconflict transition remains fragile, and the reconciliation between Damascus and Kurdish militants in the northeast may owe as much to American pressure as it does to Turkey’s domestic efforts to make peace with the PKK. But for Turkey, the eventual integration of Syrian Kurdish forces into the Syrian state removes the risk Ankara saw in having an autonomous, armed Kurdish entity on its southern border. And, given the close security and economic ties Ankara has developed with Damascus, as well as the political and legal steps the government can take at home to complete the disbanding of the PKK and to deepen democratic reforms, Turkey has the ability to keep these encouraging developments on track.

    According to recent reports, turkey’s regional policies are most successful when the country plays to its strengths—not when it is trying to throw its weight around the region. In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Ankara built real influence by mediating between Syria and Israel and between Palestinian factions, expanding its economic engagement in the Levant, and proposing projects to connect the region’s energy and transportation infrastructure. Military power, meanwhile, has proved most effective when applied for specific purposes, such as to secure the border with Syria. This combination is Turkey’s winning formula: diplomacy and economic outreach to extend its influence, and limited force to protect its core interests. Broad, open-ended commitments, by contrast, risk drawing Turkey into regional conflicts without making it safer.

    Industry observers note that today, sticking to a more effective formula does not mean retreating from regional politics. It means setting priorities and planning long-term. Consolidating the Kurdish peace process, keeping Washington invested in Syria’s stabilization, managing the risk of confrontation with Israel in Syria, and maintaining constructive relations with the Kurdistan Regional Government in northern Iraq and the Iraqi government in Baghdad are key to keeping Turkey’s borders secure and are within Turkey’s ability to achieve. Ankara can continue to use its experience in mediation when opportunities to advance peace processes present themselves. It can also promote economic connectivity, both by expanding trade ties and by supporting regional infrastructure projects such as the Iraq-Europe Development Road and a proposed pipeline network connecting the Gulf to Jordan, Syria, and Turkey. It need not shy away from security cooperation with the Gulf, either, if it can engage without making formal commitments. Yet in all these endeavors, Ankara should remember that it has the most clout when it stays out of the region’s conflicts.

    The Middle East’s escalating wars and rival blocs could make a narrower Turkish security policy more difficult to sustain today than it was in the past. Defending Ankara’s interests and playing a constructive role in a volatile neighborhood will require a careful balance. The best way Turkey can contribute to regional stability may be to avoid trying to do too much.

    #145282. Pop Culture Still Can’t Figure Out Drone Warfare

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2124 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    Pop Culture Still Can’t Figure Out Drone Warfare

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore.
    • According to recent reports, hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo.
    • Military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    In a recent development, military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore. They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

    According to recent reports, hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light shows. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

    Military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore. They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

    In a recent development, hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light reveals. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

    In a recent development, but perhaps the makers of Lioness deserve some credit simply for tackling the subject. Four and a half years after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, cultural depictions of how the war is actually being fought are strikingly thin on the ground. A few journalists have written solid first-person accounts of the conflict, and documentary filmmakers, many of them Ukrainian, have explored it with astonishing intimacy. Yet their works have reached relatively small audiences. Where are the gripping stories for the broader public?

    In a recent development, combat drones have certainly made a mark on the broader culture. You see them everywhere, from movies like The Terminal List: Dark Wolf , where an assassin uses a drone to blow up a car, to the BBC’s police procedural Vigil, which includes a sequence in which military drones are turned against their own side by a hostile hacker. It’s striking how often drones turn up in dystopian science fiction films—such as The Gorge, where two snipers fight off autonomous drones, and The Outer Threat, in which a man with a dramatic secret has to protect his family from a hostile government equipped with drone swarms. A few years ago, the drone designs in these films probably would have resembled the exquisitely engineered aircraft of the so-called global war on terror. Now, even sci-fi creators seem to be favoring small quadcopters like the ones used by Ukrainians in their fight against Russia. But few of these cultural references involve depictions of war.

    In a recent development, retired Australian Army Maj. Gen. Mick Ryan, who has carefully tracked the war in Ukraine, argues that pop culture can be a useful way of helping politicians and the public stay abreast of developments on the battlefield. “Military doctrine is inaccessible to most people, including a lot of people in the military,” he mentioned. “Whether it’s movies, television, books, or podcasts, [pop culture] can be an excellent way of making complex military and technological intersections accessible to a broader range of people.” Ryan practices what he preaches: He’s written an excellent speculative novel, White Sun War, about a hypothetical conflict over Taiwan, which includes detailed scenes of Chinese and U.S. forces fighting with the help of autonomous unmanned ground vehicles. Ryan’s fictional technology is ahead of what the Russians and Ukrainians have developed in their war—but only slightly.

    A Ukrainian soldier fires at a drone flying overhead in Kramatorsk, Ukraine, on Nov. 11. Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images.

    Could it be that drone warfare is just too complicated for compelling storytelling? By now, both sides in the Russia-Ukraine war have deployed a wide variety of drones on land, at sea, and in the air. None of these machines exists in isolation. They’re part of complex battlefield ecosystems that encompass reconnaissance, strike, and (increasingly) supply. Lately the Ukrainians have even been using ground drones to evacuate wounded soldiers. The intensity of the conflict has driven an astonishing pace of innovation, often involving the intricacies of maintaining reliable communications and targeting in environments saturated with electronic warfare measures. Responses have included drones controlled by fiber-optic cables (which can’t be jammed, unlike radio signals) and increasing reliance on artificial intelligence systems that can keep drones on target even when their links with operators go down.

    In a recent development, perhaps it’s no surprise that outsiders have a hard time keeping up. In October, video game publisher Activision released Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the latest installment of its long-running franchise. (A reminder: The global gaming industry is way bigger than the movie industry.) The story revolves around an imagined North Korean invasion of South Korea, and its depiction of the intense combat that such a conflict would entail is amazingly convincing. The game’s creators have put a huge amount of effort into getting the details right (even extending to hiring a dialect coach to consult on the different forms of Korean spoken by the characters).

    Recent findings suggest that seeing the effort the game’s designers put into verisimilitude, it’s all the more surprising that drones have a very limited role. This omission is especially odd given that North Korea has dispatched large numbers of troops to help Russia in the war against Ukraine—in part so that Kim Jong Un’s forces could learn about the intricacies of drone warfare. The game’s creators seem to have been oblivious to this. When a joint South Korean-U.S. force counters the invasion with an amphibious counterattack, the intensity of the combat recalls the opening scenes of Saving Private Ryan. Yet neither side in the fight deploys drones on land or in the sky—although this is exactly the sort of combat in which modern militaries are already working frantically to incorporate the lessons of Ukraine.

    In 1983, two movies sought to educate and alarm the public about the risks of new technologies.

    From the president on down, many Americans still do not grasp the implications of drones and other threats.

    Part of the problem is surely that the remote-controlled, seemingly anonymous nature of modern drones diminishes their narrative potential. Real-life drone operations often involve long and meticulous searches and extended loitering—not exactly the stuff of high drama. Those brutal Ukrainian drone attack videos that now populate social media show only the climactic moments that follow hours and hours of painstaking preparation and reconnaissance. This could be why we see some video game designers creating drones with machine guns on them; in real life, that’s a generally useless approach, since the recoil from the guns would destabilize the drone, perhaps fatally. But shooting feels a lot more satisfying than hitting a distant target that you can only see on a screen.

    Industry observers note that that video games present such a distorted vision of contemporary war is especially ironic considering that the gaming industry has significantly shaped drone warfare. Military drone controllers are often modeled on the ones used by gamers, which hugely simplifies training.

    Sources indicate that ukrainian filmmakers have found themselves confronting similar narrative challenges. The fascinating latest movie Killhouse, which was shot in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military, features plenty of scenes that convey a vivid sense of the peculiarities of drone warfare. The film turns on the fate of a civilian couple who are lured into the gray zone between the front lines by Russian gangsters who are holding their daughter for ransom. Unlike the blissful U.S. soldiers in Lioness, the desperate mother and father are immediately detected by both the Russians and Ukrainians as soon as they enter the area. The Russians promptly shell them, while the Ukrainians devise a complicated, drone-assisted strategy for their rescue—and, ultimately, the daughter’s. One particularly nail-biting sequence depicts an operator trying to use a drone to guide a character through a minefield, even though he has no clear way of communicating with her.

    The movie’s creators would have done well to stop there, after showing us real-life drones in real-life situations. Unfortunately, even they apparently felt the need to juice up their story by introducing a set of as-yet-non-existent drones that use facial recognition systems for their targets. (That capability is pretty useful for the Chinese surveillance state; why you would need it on a battlefield without expansive access to a database of enemy faces remains unclear.) At the moment of a critical showdown, these ultra-high-tech drones are used simply as brute force to knock out several Russian soldiers—all that fancy equipment ends up effectively serving the same purpose as a couple of massive rocks.

    Recent findings suggest that perhaps the shortcomings of movies and video games aren’t worth taking so seriously. There’s no requirement for ultra-realism, and no one should exaggerate the extent to which popular culture drives the decisions of policymakers. But is it just a coincidence that Western militaries, policymakers, and politicians are still failing to learn from the war in Ukraine after all these years?

    A still from Killhouse. Ukrainian Film Division.

    U.S. and other Western military bases are still plagued by drone incursions of unknown provenance; the one thing that’s clear is that many of these drones, which are equipped to resist powerful jamming, aren’t operated by hobbyists. In recent weeks, the U.S. Air Force has cited the threat of drone attacks in connection with at least two major alerts at air bases in Britain. Decision-makers were apparently reacting to fears that Iran might launch an attack emulating Kyiv’s stunning Operation Spiderweb, when Ukraine managed to destroy a number of Russian strategic bombers by launching drones that were smuggled into Russia on freight trucks. European NATO members have experienced various drone incursions, as well as confronting actual attacks. Even the Australians have had to deal with mysterious drone sightings near their bases. The technology is proliferating; the problem can no longer be written off.

    According to recent reports, we’re still waiting for the Hollywood blockbuster that brings home the impact of drone warfare to ordinary voters—something like the 1927 film Wings, one of the first to familiarize a broad audience with the significance of military aircraft. But the lack of popular familiarity with the changed nature of war is no excuse for the complacency of Western leaders.

    Recent findings suggest that christian Caryl is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a former Moscow bureau chief for Newsweek and U.S. News & World Report, and the author of Strange Rebels: 1979 and the Birth of the 21st Century. X: @ccaryl.
